idea: Context management pays most when the window is tight; its gain shrinks as the window grows and vanishes when the window is ample, so measure the gain at your own window size.
best_evidence: Management gain on SWE-Bench fell 35.7, 15.9, 5.5, 2.7 points from 32k to 128k window (2609.20804 page 7); minus 0.3 at 262,144 tokens (2608.26218)
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, including one with Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 showing no threshold effect; mostly open models, one run per task
why: Newest paper adds strong one-million-token models where compaction threshold from 160K to 380K changed nothing, while the smallest-window model lost at low thresholds. Shape is consistent across five papers; no contrary measurement.

idea: When the task fits the window, compressing or filtering history on strong models saves tokens but does not raise accuracy and often costs a few points; judge compression by billed cost and score together.
models: Qwen3.7-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol
best_evidence: Compression lowered ProgramBench by 4.86 points for Qwen3.7-Max and 3.85 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro (2609.32459 page 9); full history 0.63 against summarizer 0.59 on SWE-bench (2611.06445 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: many papers agree, but most are single runs or two runs, authors' own harnesses, differences of a few points
why: Eight papers from May to November show no accuracy gain or a small loss from compression or history filtering, and a billed-cost saving that is smaller than token counts suggest. The only gain against is an April study on older models.

idea: On long tasks that outgrow the window, one continuous conversation with summarized old turns and a note-taking instruction scores far above a stateless default setup.
models: GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GPT-OSS-120B
best_evidence: Summary with notes scored a mean 63.08 against 9.24 for the standard setup on four ARC-AGI-3 games (2610.26632 page 7)
evidence_quality: weak: ARC-AGI-3 games, one run per setup, unequal limits between arms, part of the gap from other changes
why: Three October papers agree on the sign with strong hosted models; the size is inflated by unequal budgets and single runs, so trust direction only. The ladder in 2610.02200 shows conversation alone adds about 14 points of 51.66 to 65.82.

idea: A truncated or summarized window drops facts the agent cannot observe again; keep such facts in persistent state or make them re-readable, because the model cannot recover them.
models: gpt-6-luna, claude-haiku-5-5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6
best_evidence: Truncated window succeeded on 15 of 200 when the fact could not be re-observed against 200 of 200 with full history (2610.26632 page 4)
evidence_quality: medium: two providers with intervals, but a synthetic probe the authors built; summary test is a planted-fact probe
why: Replicated on two providers and in a summary test where 106 of 108 summaries kept none of ten planted facts without a memory tier. When the lost fact can be fetched again the window works, so the risk is facts that exist nowhere else.

idea: Compaction summaries lose instructions, rules and scope limits, and an agent that keeps the rule still breaks it more often than one with full history; persist rules outside the conversation and re-inject them.
best_evidence: Rule violation at three runs rose from 9.6 percent with full history to 37.8 percent after compaction (2611.03223 page 6); 36.8 percent of scope exclusions dropped (2610.31778 page 8)
evidence_quality: medium: matched full-history baseline and two papers agree, but authors' own benchmark, three runs per case, mostly cheap models
why: Two papers from late October and November measure the loss against a full-history control. Loss varies by model: Opus 4.6 dropped 0.51 rule categories per compaction, GPT-5.3-Codex 2.73. Test the compaction step, not only the final score.

idea: Compaction machinery fails silently in practice: results replaced by notices, tool calls during compaction, recap injected on only some compactions, and weaker models never calling a self-managed compaction tool.
models: Gemma 4 31B, Claude Opus 5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Nemotron Super
best_evidence: Recap injected at only 21 of 45 compactions on Modal and 50 of 77 on Kaggle (2611.19359 page 6)
evidence_quality: weak: failure counts in authors' own benchmarks, mostly single runs, no controlled comparison of fixes
why: Five papers from April to November observe the same class of failure, including Haiku 5.5 never calling the compaction tool in six sessions and a default Claude Code window never compacting Opus 5.5. Log and test whether compaction fired and what it kept.

idea: On strong models with very large windows, the default self-summarization is as good as engineered compaction strategies; a cheaper summarizer or discarding reasoning hurt two of three models.
best_evidence: No compaction strategy beat default self-summarization beyond the intervals on any benchmark; GPT-5.4 fell 0.59 to 0.43 with a small-model summary (2610.31778 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: independent-style study across three benchmarks and three models, but two runs per task and one agent program
why: Newest paper on strong models finds no tuning headroom in summarization strategy, and compression count did not correlate with score in 2608.05013 (r minus 0.034). Spend effort on what summaries keep, not on the strategy.

idea: With small open models, compaction details matter by 8 to 12 points: trigger timing, clearing tool output before summarizing, and per-model calibration; one policy's sign flipped between two models.
best_evidence: Summarization resolve rate rose 50.7 to 62.7 percent by delaying the trigger from 10,000 to 20,000 tokens; clearing before summarizing added 7.7, 9.7, 9.7 points (2609.32961 pages 7, 9)
evidence_quality: medium: three runs per policy, 65 policies, 35,000 executions; small models, coding only, thresholds tied to model
why: Largest controlled study of compaction policy, three runs each. Terminal-Bench still lost 5 to 13 points on 11 of 12 policies, and totals hide turnover of gained and lost tasks, so repeat runs.

idea: Replacing old tool outputs with a placeholder is as good as model summarization and cheaper.
best_evidence: Clearing at threshold gave 53.7 percent resolve rate at 0.57 times tokens on SWE-bench but 11 of 12 policies lost 5 to 13 points on Terminal-Bench (2609.32961 pages 6, 9)
evidence_quality: medium: replayed or repeated runs support it on SWE-bench, but the same paper shows Terminal-Bench losses and others find clearing hurts
why: Clearing wins on one coding set and in a cost replay, loses on a terminal set, and a Sonnet 4.5 research study found clearing lowered accuracy. No regime split explains all three.

idea: Cutting tool output by character position deletes whole evidence fields and breaks results silently; cut by record or keep results re-readable, and replay recorded results through the cut to check.
best_evidence: 3,827 of 11,189 field tool results were cut and every cut result broke (2610.36114 page 2)
evidence_quality: weak: one harness and domain, model unstated, 15 runs per arm, accuracy link noisy; authors wrote the defect
why: Measured cut damage is large and checkable without a model. The accuracy effect is noisy, and only one paper tests it on real field data.

idea: When material fits in context, give it inline; adding an index, summary tree or search layer in front lowers accuracy for weaker models, is neutral for the strongest, and weaker agents often never use the search.
models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6
best_evidence: Reading a report through a section index cost GPT-5.1 11.3 points, interval minus 18.0 to minus 4.9 (2610.26836 page 4); strongest models showed no change
evidence_quality: medium: intervals shown in one paper and three more agree, but varied tasks, author-written items, single episodes in some
why: Six papers from August to November find retrieval or index layers neutral or harmful where the material would fit, including search started in only 28.9 percent of runs. A missed policy section raised violations to 17.1 from 10.3 percent.

idea: When material is too large to read, a structure-aware code index or retrieval tool raises localization and pass rates, with the lift largest for weaker models.
best_evidence: Retrieval raised pass rate on all four models, 9.5 points on average; qwen3.6-flash 73 to 86 percent (2609.04898 page 5)
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, one with paired tests, but mostly single runs on authors' harnesses
why: Lift of 86 percent for Gemma-4-31B against 2 percent for GPT-5.5 on one codebase (2610.28802). Model-free file selection alone found only 56 of 108 vulnerable flows (2610.38617), so retrieval recall bounds the result.

idea: Keeping task state, evidence or notes in a persistent record outside the transcript raises results for mid-strength models, with a searchable or curated record beating raw history at lower cost; the strongest models gain less.
best_evidence: Mean reciprocal rank on Defects4J rose from 0.323 to 0.633 for GLM-5 with persistent evidence state (2610.23996 page 2); full history cost 0.315 dollars against 0.140 for a notebook (2610.00675)
evidence_quality: medium: seven papers agree across tasks, but authors' own systems and mostly single runs; Opus 4.8 showed no effect in one
why: Seven papers agree. The same paper that shows the largest gain found no effect on Opus 4.8, so the lift shrinks with model strength.

idea: Piling more memory, rules or recap into the prompt gives no reliable gain and raises tokens per turn; gains decay as entries accumulate unless scoped, tested and pruned, and more retrieved entries can lower sequential task success.
models: gpt-5.6-luna, Gemma 4 31B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5
best_evidence: Gain fell from plus 0.017 to minus 0.016 as active rules grew from 13 to 70, with input tokens 1.50 to 2.52 times baseline (2609.24130 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, but one seed or few runs, small effects, authors' own systems
why: Memory added about 2,000 tokens to every request (2611.19359) and extra context strategies lowered scores in 2605.06177. Tested, pruned memory still helped in some papers, so the warning is about unvalidated accumulation.

idea: Facts the model cannot derive from code or the first message, such as team decisions, domain rules and earlier session intent, must be supplied as context; general knowledge did not substitute.
models: Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, gpt-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6 Sol
best_evidence: Task writer given the full work episode covered 75 percent of requirements against 26 percent from the first message on multi-session tasks (2611.02440 page 11)
evidence_quality: medium: six papers across code, payments, health and task writing, large effects, but authors built the tasks to expose the gap
why: Open-book rules lifted Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview from 14.6 to 89.6 (2609.18270). Source code access alone lifted only 18.6 to 29.6 percent (2610.20779), so supply the decisions, not only more code.

idea: After a failed attempt, pass compact feedback on what failed; neither the full earlier reasoning nor a clean restart from an empty workspace performs best.
best_evidence: Rebuilding from an empty workspace each loop lowered GameCraft-Bench from 71.52 to 63.67 and raised tokens from 8.41M to 11.12M (2609.01481 page 14)
evidence_quality: weak: different tasks, mostly single runs; the compact-feedback ablation has intervals of about 20 points
why: Direction agrees from a frontier model to tiny models, where clean restart raised repeated failed calls from 31 to 80 percent. Against is one argued March claim with a 3 percent gain.

idea: Load instructions and skills for the current phase, chosen by the harness, rather than all at once or at the model's discretion; full injection costs more in later phases.
models: GPT-5.5, Doubao-2.0-Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.6
best_evidence: Current-phase-only instructions beat full-protocol injection by 2.1 points early, 6.2 middle and 10.4 late (2609.39551 page 10); stage context cut invalid information used from 11 of 30 to 0 of 30
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, models partly unstated, one benchmark each, runs unstated
why: Harness-chosen skill entry scored 83.6 against 65.6 for model-chosen (2608.24876). Against: preloading full skill text barely changed skill-use scores once both modes triggered (2608.04828). Skills also overrode correct readings (2607.22520).

idea: A large fixed prefix, such as full tool schemas or a long preamble, and large tool output fed back raise tokens per task with no measured accuracy benefit.
models: Claude Opus 5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash
best_evidence: Fixed preamble 16,581 tokens in Claude Code against 829 in mini-SWE-agent with equivalent success on 447 tasks (2610.04433 page 8); 44 tool schemas cost 3.1 times tokens (2608.08654)
evidence_quality: medium: six papers agree on tokens; accuracy parity rests on one run per cell and authors' cost counts
why: Retrieving tools cut schema tokens 99.8 percent (2606.16591). A 30,000-byte output cap showed no cost change, and the paper never proved the cap fired (2609.11987). Dollar cost is a separate question, see the cache idea.

idea: Dollar cost per task follows the number of turns and prefix cache hits more than prompt size; flat token counts overstate cost several times, so judge changes by billed cost with caching.
best_evidence: Turn count explains 84 percent of variance in log cost, mean observation size 4 percent; flat pricing overstates cost 7.14 times (2610.15093 pages 5, 6)
evidence_quality: weak: simulated replay of published trajectories, assumed cache and weak-model price; later papers observe cache-read shares of 99.9 percent
why: Cache hits were 98.1 to 99.0 percent of input tokens in replay, and routing saving fell from 23 to 8 percent with long user pauses (2609.28919). Rewriting history breaks the cache and loses the saving.

idea: Splitting work across subagents or stages helps only when each gets a complete task-specific brief and returns a bounded report; generic delegation or lossy hand-offs drop essentials and hurt.
best_evidence: Task-specific subagents added 5.91 points on ProgramBench for Qwen3.7-Max while general subagents lost 0.70 (2609.32459 page 9)
evidence_quality: weak: one benchmark without repeats for the component split; others single run or observed, authors' own harnesses
why: Worker prompts kept answer options in at most 5 of 125 (2603.10044); 98 workers passed nothing and silence read as nothing found (2610.36114). Workflow context stayed bounded near 11,000 to 47,000 tokens over a 789-call run (2610.35349).

idea: Splitting a very long input across fresh sub-agent harnesses beats a single coding agent on long-context aggregation tasks.
best_evidence: Prime Agent with Opus 5 beat Claude Code on six of nine rows but lost OOLONG .900 against .920 and EmulatorBench .047 against .062 (2608.23552 page 7)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own harnesses, baselines copied or unmatched, no bare model, repeats unstated
why: Wins on six rows and losses on three in one paper; the other paper's GPT-5 design fell below its comparison at some lengths (53.3 percent at 1M against Codex 71.75). No regime split found.

idea: Agents and models degrade as input grows well before the window is full, so late turns break instructions that the early ones followed.
models: GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5
best_evidence: Eighteen frontier models degraded as input grew, starting around 50K (ext-agent-harness-engineering-survey-openreview, cited measurement)
evidence_quality: weak: older models, a cited survey figure and a one-model probe; no test separates length from task difficulty
why: Measured only on April to June models; a September study found repository size not the main bottleneck for strong agents, and compaction papers show loss from summaries, not from length alone. Not re-tested on current models.

idea: A context harness added only after training recovers little of the benefit of training with it in place; train or tune small models inside the harness they will run in.
best_evidence: Removing the harness at evaluation dropped unseen ALFWorld success from 63.43 to 40.30 (2610.02858 Table 2); training-time beat post-hoc by 20.7 to 22.5 points (2606.25447)
evidence_quality: weak: three papers on small models and toy tasks, single runs, authors' systems
why: Training on a compressed stream also drifts from the rollout (0.366 against floor 0.014, 2609.00865). Only matters if you train models; not tested on hosted models.

idea: Harness search and debugging work best from raw execution traces; scores or summaries of traces gave far less.
best_evidence: Median 50.0 with raw traces against 34.6 scores only and 34.9 scores plus summary (2603.28052 Table 3)
evidence_quality: medium: same table in two papers, but one benchmark and proposer; later paper is a different method
why: Measured on one task set with Opus 4.6 as proposer, before September; the October paper found both successes and failures help, not raw traces specifically. Not re-tested on current models.

idea: With the model fixed, swapping the harness changes cost per solved task by roughly 3 to 40 times, far more than tool interface or small prompt changes do.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Sonnet 5, gpt-5.6-terra
best_evidence: 2607.22585 Table 3: Goose 28,142 and OpenCode 1,147,740 tokens per solved task on one model, about 40 times apart.
evidence_quality: strong: nine independent studies on many models agree; mostly one run per cell, no bare baseline in most
why: Every paper comparing harnesses on one model found large cost gaps, newest dated 2026-10-24. Size depends on vendor pairing: Codex against Claude Code differed 5.9 to 10.2 times on Claude models, near parity on GPT.

idea: More tokens, calls or spend inside a harness do not reliably buy higher success; across models and harnesses, spend and score are barely related.
models: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol
best_evidence: 2611.08946 page 11: rank correlation of -0.05 between relative token use and score across 12 models.
evidence_quality: medium: a dozen papers agree across tasks; correlational, model and harness vary together, several benchmarks built by authors
why: Newest measurement dated 2026-11-12 on strong models shows no link; the two contrary papers found weak positive links (one argued only, one rank correlation 0.23 for tokens).

idea: On strong Claude models, raising reasoning effort from low to medium or high buys large score gains; beyond high it flattens, and very low effort can even run slower.
models: Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5
best_evidence: 2611.05512 page 9 Table 4: Claude Opus 4.7 scored 48.80 percent at low, 56.49 medium, 67.62 high effort.
evidence_quality: medium: four benchmarks agree on Claude models; authors built the benchmarks, runs per cell mostly unstated or few
why: Four measurements from 2026-08 to 2026-11 on Claude models show low-to-high gains; the plateau is shown by 12 of 25 low, 19 high, 17 extra high for Sonnet 5. GPT models showed no such gain, see next idea.

idea: Raising reasoning effort above the middle setting on GPT models, or from high to max on Kimi K3, multiplies time and tokens for little or no mean score change.
models: GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Kimi-K3
best_evidence: 2611.07238 page 14: going from High to Max reasoning adds 0.80 million tokens with no measurable gain on Kimi-K3.
evidence_quality: medium: three papers of 2026-10 and 2026-11 agree; small differences, few repeats, authors' own benchmarks
why: Split of the first-pass effort idea by model family: GPT and Kimi plateau (newest 2026-11-07), while Claude models gain from low to high. The two contrary papers measured low against high on Claude.

idea: Cutting context saves money only when the prompt cache stays intact and what is dropped is chosen with care; blind truncation or token-count targets can raise the billed cost.
models: claude-haiku-5-5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Kimi K3
best_evidence: 2610.26632 page 6: a truncated window cost 3.3 to 3.7 times billed cost per episode while sending 0.84 to 0.90 times the tokens.
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree; open-weight models in the largest study, authors' own probes, costs partly estimated under assumed cache pricing
why: Papers through 2026-11-04 agree token count misleads: dropped turns break the cache, 0.6 times tokens still gave 0.71 to 0.95 times the bill, and self-managed compaction cut cost 16 to 58 percent on two models.

idea: A harness that trims waste, with shorter outputs, fewer calls, leaner orchestration or pruned prompts, can cut cost per task by about 17 to 60 percent at equal or higher success, if success is rechecked.
best_evidence: 2610.00885 page 7: on claude-opus-5 at extra high effort, strict successes rose 89 to 96 while total cost fell from $135 to $111.
evidence_quality: medium: a dozen papers agree on strong models; mostly authors' own harness against a generic loop, one run per condition
why: Measured repeatedly through 2026-11-09 on strong models, but 2610.30499 found nine of 27 cheaper harness lineages lost held-out score, so a cut needs its own success check; savings often compare against a generic baseline.

idea: Harness layers that add checking, repair, gates, controllers or evolution usually raise cost per attempt by about 1.2 to 1.8 times, so their extra success must be judged per solved task.
best_evidence: 2609.24130 page 7: harness runs cost 1.72 times the unmodified agent loop overall, including $92.90 of repair spend.
evidence_quality: medium: a dozen papers agree, several with bare baselines and repeated trials; small task counts, own systems
why: Newest evidence 2026-11-09 is a null result. Two papers found some mechanisms cost no more than plain OpenCode or a bare agent, so the rule holds for added loops and controllers, not every layer.

idea: Verifying once or selectively (one independent verifier, a closeout check) costs about 1.1 to 1.3 times; checking every step or gating completion costs 1.5 to 3.4 times, and a reviewer can dominate a run.
best_evidence: 2610.30284 page 5: all-step verification 75.27 percent at 3.35 times cost, selective verification 77.20 percent at 1.09 times on MiniMax-M2.7.
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, one with same-model baseline; own systems, gains inside run spread, hand-tuned thresholds
why: Newest 2026-11-06; reviews took a median 13.8 percent of cost in one paper and 75 percent in another, depending on cadence. First-pass idea narrowed to placement of the check.

idea: A cheap or small model in a tuned harness can reach most of a frontier model's score at a small fraction of the cost per task.
models: gemma-4-26b-a4b, gemini-3.1-pro-preview, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Composer-2.5
best_evidence: 2607.08938 page 8: best small model with optimized harness reached 89 percent of frontier accuracy (80.2 versus 89.7) at 4 percent of cost per instance.
evidence_quality: medium: eleven papers agree across tasks; mostly authors' tuned harness, few runs, contrary papers measure tokens or a mini model
why: Papers dated 2026-09 to 2026-11 keep showing cheaper models matching or beating pricier ones per result, for example $0.075 per case against $1.082 for GPT-5.5; the contrary cases used a mini model or counted tokens, not dollars.

idea: A cheaper model per token is not always cheaper per solved task: weaker or open-weight models use 2 to 4 times the tokens, and higher success can make a pricier model cheaper per success.
models: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 5, Fable 5.1, GPT 5.4
best_evidence: 2610.02459 page 35: cost per success $93.3 for Sonnet 5, $18.9 for Opus 5, $11.2 for Fable 5.1.
evidence_quality: medium: one large study of 6,627 tasks plus smaller ones; success rates differ widely, some figures are estimates
why: Newest 2026-11-09. Weaker models still cost 2 to 3 times less per trial in the large study, so this narrows rather than reverses the cheap-model idea; one paper shows 13 of 18 small pairings costing more tokens per solve.

idea: Cost claims need cost per solved task from checked usage: per-attempt cost, token counts, flat input pricing or list-price weights mislead, and one telemetry bug overstated a harness cost 5 to 8 times.
best_evidence: 2609.11987 page 6: a cache-token double count overstated deepagents cost roughly 5 to 8 times.
evidence_quality: medium: nine papers with concrete audits; small pools, one run per condition in several, one result simulated
why: Each paper shows a headline figure that moves under another accounting: flat pricing overstated loop cost 7.14 times under cache hits, and changing token weights shifted a cost effect threefold. Newest 2026-11-09.

idea: Token use is heavily right-skewed and failed or looping runs consume most of it, so averages hide the cost and caps or early stops belong on the failure tail.
models: DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview, MiniMax M3, Kimi K2.7, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
best_evidence: 2610.32483 page 16: mean token use exceeds the median in 89 of 90 cells; the top 5 percent of Qwen-Pi runs use about 83 percent of tokens.
evidence_quality: strong: 90 cells, four repetitions, four models; independent studies agree; measures tokens, not money
why: Studies through 2026-11-12 agree: unresolved tasks used 2.7 times the tokens of resolved ones, timeouts took 14 of 22.4 hours, and one model hit the time limit in 51 of 120 attempts. Net saving from caps was not tested.

idea: At matched compute, harness gains often shrink or vanish against simply sampling more attempts, though some papers still find a structured harness ahead of equal retries.
best_evidence: 2607.12227 page 6: at five rollouts, parallel sampling scored 72.3 against 67.4 for harness evolution on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
evidence_quality: medium: twelve papers with mixed baselines; two-run averages, authors' own systems, no shared definition of matched budget
why: Papers of similar date and quality split: sampling matched or beat evolved harnesses in six, while a planned harness beat eight sampled runs at 1.12 times compute (64.7 against 73.3) and a loop beat plain passes.

idea: Automatic harness optimization costs tens to a few hundred dollars per model and task set and pays back only after repeated use; headline savings often leave that cost out.
best_evidence: 2607.08938 page 8: $20 per model and task pair, recovered after about 13 runs on average.
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own optimizers, small task counts, payback computed by the authors
why: Papers report optimizer costs from $37.02 to $367.86, newest 2026-11-03; one states its headline savings exclude optimizer calls. No contrary measurement, but all rest on the authors' own systems.

idea: Routing steps or sessions to cheaper models is reported to save 13 to 90 percent, but per-request switching can break the prompt cache and delegation raised cost in half of simulated settings.
best_evidence: 2609.28919 page 12: cache-aware routing cut simulated enterprise model spend by 13 to 21 percent.
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own routers, simulated or one-run results; the opposing paper is also simulated on open-weight models
why: Merges the first-pass routing idea. Savings are simulated or single-run (10.9 times on one benchmark); a naive per-request switch cost 5.1 percent more and a pre-screen saved only 4.3 percent once counted.

idea: A harness pays back most per dollar on weaker or cheaper models; on the strongest models its extra cost is harder to recover, though some papers show strong models saving too.
best_evidence: 2607.25566 page 8: moving to the fixed loop bought 3.8 and 6.0 accuracy points per dollar on two cheap models, against 0.5 on GPT-5.5.
evidence_quality: medium: seven papers, mixed tasks; ten-task and 22-task samples, one run per condition in several
why: Cost on the strongest tier rose in three papers (Fable 5 from $0.29 to $2.13 per task) but fell on GPT-5.5 and Opus 5 in two others; no regime split explains it. Newest 2026-10-24.

idea: Billed cost of an agent run follows the number of turns and tool calls, each re-reading a cached prefix, not the size of single observations, so cutting turns pays more than trimming outputs.
best_evidence: 2610.15093 page 1: turn count explains 84 percent of variance in log cost, mean observation size 4 percent.
evidence_quality: weak: first paper simulated from published trajectories on open-weight models; second is the authors' own platform, associational
why: Two papers dated 2026-10-10 and 2026-11-09 agree: tool calls raised cost 1.6 to 26 times at similar token counts and cache reads were 53 to 73 percent of cost on long contexts. No contrary result found.

idea: When the bare model already answers the task in one call, an agent loop multiplies cost about 2 to 100 times for no gain; reserve loops for tasks the bare model cannot do.
best_evidence: 2609.38137 page 6: a recursive loop scored 2 percent at $7.86 where direct reading scored 44 percent at $0.780.
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, one with a bare run; author-built tasks, no repeats, estimated list-price costs
why: Newest 2026-09-29 on GPT-5.6-sol: 94 percent direct at $0.648 against 96 percent in OpenCode at $1.37. The contrary paper had a bare model that mostly failed, so the loop paid there.

idea: Moving repeated steps from model calls into fixed code, compiled behaviors or batched calls cuts cost or latency by about 10 to 25 times at the same success.
best_evidence: 2609.29166 page 27: 1134.9 seconds per Swap rollout against 49.2 seconds, 23.1 times faster, after compiling a task into fixed code.
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, mixed tasks, mostly single runs or copied baselines; latency counted more than money
why: Eight papers from 2026-04 to 2026-11-05 agree, for example composing primitives cost 4.3 percent of one actor attempt and batching fifteen questions cost 12 times less. None found it failed to save.

idea: Harness search can score candidates on a subset, race them or cascade them, cutting search evaluation cost about 40 to 60 percent while picking the same or a near-equal harness.
models: Kimi-K2.5, GLM-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.6 Luna
best_evidence: 2609.05903 page 8: cascade cut evaluation tokens 43.6 percent and chose the same harness in 22 of 22 candidate banks.
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own methods, small task counts, one run, no outside replication
why: Seven papers from 2026-05 to 2026-10 agree, newest 2026-10-27, with 40 percent of validation cost giving near-full selection quality; none tested whether the saved evaluations hurt harnesses on tasks never seen.

idea: A single run on tens of tasks cannot separate harnesses: swapping the harness flips about as many tasks as rerunning the same harness, so gaps of a few points are noise.
best_evidence: 13% of hard tasks flip under a harness swap, the same as under a rerun; 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap half the time (2610.04433 page 3)
evidence_quality: strong: many independent studies, reruns measured directly, several models; most grid cells are still single runs
why: Newest measurements (October, November) agree and none disagrees. Reruns of the same harness give the noise floor, so budget repeats and enough tasks before claiming a gain.

idea: A harness gain measured on the tasks that guided its search overstates the held-out gain; much of it is overfitting or extra compute, so always report a separate held-out split.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
best_evidence: In 21 settings with significant search gains, overfitting is 54% and extra test-time compute 14% of the gain (2610.22466 page 6)
evidence_quality: strong: ten papers, many models and tasks; protocols often built by the authors, repeated runs rarely stated
why: Newest measurements (October, November) on recent models show held-out gain below search gain, sometimes zero. None shows equal gain on both. Papers do not report bare-model success, so regime is unclear.

idea: An automatically evolved harness keeps a positive gain over its starting harness on held-out tasks.
models: GPT-5.6-Terra, GPT-6-sol, GPT-5.6 Luna, Claude Opus 4.6
best_evidence: For: held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1 81.00 against 66.33 for the seed harness (2611.05139 page 7). Against: 63.2 against 63.2 on 34 tasks (2607.12227 page 7)
evidence_quality: medium: results of equal date disagree; mostly single runs, authors' own systems, starting harness often weak
why: Positive results compare with the authors' own starting harness; null results use equal-compute or direct baselines or strong models. Baseline success is unreported, so no regime split could be shown.

idea: A fuller harness beats a minimal one by about 8 to 13 points on a fixed model, so harness variance outweighs model variance.
models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-sol, Grok 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview
best_evidence: Claude Code minus mini-SWE-agent on 447 tasks: -1.8 and -1.4 points, equivalent (2610.04433 page 5); earlier: +13.0 for GLM-5.1 (2605.23950 page 7)
evidence_quality: medium: later studies agree but use different minimal harnesses; mostly single runs; earlier study had 100 tasks, two runs
why: May study found minimal-to-full gains of 8.5 to 13.0 points. Later studies on newer models find production harnesses within noise and model explaining most variance (58% against 12%). Weak-model regime not re-tested directly.

idea: Between mature harnesses on a fixed model, pass rate differs little while cost per task differs by up to 3 times, so compare cost and tokens as well as pass rate.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5
best_evidence: Cost per task differs up to 3 times on one model while pass rate barely moves (2610.04433 page 3)
evidence_quality: medium: six papers agree on different benchmarks; mostly single runs, one paper corrected a cost double count
why: Every later measurement finds cost spread larger than pass-rate spread; none finds equal cost. The cost follows fixed preamble size and step count, not only pass rate.

idea: For a strong model the harness effect averaged over tasks is small, but it changes sign by task type, and adaptation that helps some tasks loses others, so check per-task regressions.
best_evidence: On Opus 4.8, repository tasks -9.0 [-17.2, -0.8], contest tasks +23.7 [+2.6, +44.7] (2609.11987 page 9), split chosen after seeing data
evidence_quality: medium: strong models and several papers, but small task counts and one post hoc split
why: Only the July paper found a stable gain over a plain agent, on older models. Every September to November measurement finds reversals by task or tiny averages. Newer, broader evidence wins.

idea: A mean score or final-answer score hides answer rate, partial completion, full-pass rate and task turnover, so report completion and full-pass rate next to the score.
models: GPT-5.6 Sol, gpt-6-astra, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3
best_evidence: The strongest endpoint passes 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks (2610.35138 page 8)
evidence_quality: strong: ten papers on different benchmarks agree; few repeated runs
why: Many later measurements find the headline score ranks harnesses differently from completion or full-pass checks. No paper found the mean score sufficient.

idea: Passing the functional or final-output check overstates acceptable work: many passing runs still violate policies, constraints or process steps, so add process and policy checks.
best_evidence: 162 of 175 runs passing all final numerical checks still broke another check (2610.01833 page 7)
evidence_quality: medium: ten papers agree across tasks; checks are built by the authors, few repeated runs
why: Every audit that looked found hidden violations, newest on 2026-11-11. The violation rate is per benchmark and judge, so size varies from a third to over 90 percent.

idea: Benchmark and grader defects are common and move scores by tens of points in both directions; audit tasks, oracles and scorers with a reference solution and by replay before trusting any number.
models: Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4
best_evidence: Replay correction of a reward function that never restored its database lowered pooled success from 94.3% to 65.5% (2610.16067 page 14)
evidence_quality: strong: twelve audits found concrete defects and fixed them by rerun; rates are per benchmark, not general
why: Every audit that looked found defects, newest 2026-11-14 (only 37 of 129 public tasks passed their reference fix). A reported 62.8% attack rate fell to 0% under a corrected harness.

idea: Model-judge scores shift by several points with judge choice, prompt or session, so fix and validate the judging protocol before comparing harnesses.
best_evidence: Judging protocol alone moved Gemini 3.1-Pro from 58.27 to 63.69 (2610.32332 page 7)
evidence_quality: strong: nine papers with different judges and tasks; none found judge scoring free of drift
why: Judge noise is measured repeatedly, newest in November. Validated judges can still agree with humans (next idea), so the lesson is validate and fix the protocol, not avoid judges.

idea: A judge with binary or checklist criteria, checked against human labels, agrees with humans about 85 to 93 percent of the time, so a validated judge is usable; open-ended unvalidated ones are not.
models: GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Flash
best_evidence: Judge agreed with experts on 446 of 478 decisions, 93.31% (2611.03412 page 13)
evidence_quality: medium: authors validate their own judges on small samples, usually one judge family; counter-cases use open-ended scoring
why: Judges validated against humans agree on rubric decisions in many papers; unvalidated open-ended judges disagree (alpha 0.105 in 2610.26829). The two regimes explain the disagreement, so both ideas hold.

idea: Retries, step and time limits, output caps and call counts explain a large part of reported harness gains, so compare against a bare model or direct sampling given the same budget.
models: doubao-seed-2-0-pro, Claude Sonnet-4.6, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.8
best_evidence: Retry with unchanged seed memory raised Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 32.2 to 58.6 (2608.24876 page 23)
evidence_quality: medium: nine papers, several benchmarks; mostly one author team per claim, few repeated runs
why: Equal-budget baselines repeatedly absorbed the headline gain; raising official limits alone moved GPT-5.6 Sol from 47.32 to 51.66, and 91.5% of failures ended at a harness limit. No measurement shows the budget effect vanishing.

idea: Gains on a benchmark built by the harness authors shrink on an independent benchmark, so require an outside benchmark the system was not tuned on.
best_evidence: Margin over opencode fell from +0.407 on the authors' benchmark to +0.119 on tau 2-bench (2610.02001 page 26)
evidence_quality: weak: five papers, authors' own systems, small models, single trial per task
why: Measurements from July to October agree; none shows the reverse. The evidence is thin and mostly on small models, so treat it as a strong prior, not a law.

idea: A weak or fixed-input evaluator is exploited by search or by the agent, so score with a repaired check, fresh inputs or an outside oracle.
models: Qwen3.8-27B, Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Claude Opus 4.6
best_evidence: Cached answer scored 5309 times on fixed inputs but 20 times on new input draws (2610.20673 page 5)
evidence_quality: medium: eight papers with concrete cases; small models, single kernels, few tasks
why: Newest cases are from October and none contradicts; an outside oracle closed the gap in 2607.03935. Frequency in real use is unknown.

idea: A small task subset keeps the coarse model ranking but cannot resolve harness gaps under about five points.
best_evidence: 447 tasks resolve about 5 points; 45 hard tasks catch a 13-point gap half the time (2610.04433 page 3)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers on different benchmarks; subsets chosen by the authors, few repeats
why: Subsets of 50 to 104 tasks reproduce the full-set mean or ranking, yet the newer study shows small sets cannot resolve fine gaps (rank correlation 0.13 at 7% of tasks). Different regimes, both hold.

idea: Harness uplift can be estimated without gold labels by using a stronger teacher model, until the capability gap between teacher and student is small.
best_evidence: Ceiling minus mismatch ranks harness-swap gains with Spearman 0.95 against 0.17 for frozen return change (2610.37255 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: two papers, authors' own method, small or old models, small task sets
why: Both papers (August, October) agree, including the stated limit when the gap is small. Not independently replicated and not tested on strong models, so low confidence.

idea: A gate that admits harness edits on the same visible tasks admits noise and harmful edits; gates need fresh held-out instances, a statistical margin and enough games per decision.
best_evidence: On a no-signal control, exact validation feedback reports a gain of 0.0157 while the margin contract reports 0.0033 (2610.28798 page 8)
evidence_quality: medium: nine papers; one has no language model, several are authors' own designs, few repeated runs
why: Newest evidence (late October, November) agrees: lessons that passed on gate instances failed on fresh ones, and five visible seeds bound failure far looser than 40 held-out seeds. Nothing contradicts it.

idea: Scores from different setups are not comparable: input channel, harness version, judge, answer model, token cap or user privileges each move results by points to tens of points, so report the full configuration.
models: Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 4.7, Gemini-3 Pro
best_evidence: Claude Opus 4.5 scored 45.9% under a standardized scaffold and 55.4% under Claude Code on SWE-bench Pro (2605.23950 page 2)
evidence_quality: strong: nine papers, several measured shifts; each tests one factor, mostly single runs
why: Newest measurement (2026-11-01) reorders eight models by changing only the input connection. No paper finds scores portable across setups.

idea: Evolved harness edits transfer unevenly: they can help other models, but coverage falls on other task families or distributions, so test transfer on both.
best_evidence: Transfer models gained +8.4, +7.9, +14.7, +4.7 points (2610.40721 page 8); against: coverage fell for 7 of 8 champions on the general target (2611.07624 page 9)
evidence_quality: medium: comparable-date results disagree; one run per cell, authors' own systems, different tasks
why: Transfer to other models mostly gained, transfer to other task families often lost; but papers differ in tasks and baselines and give no baseline success, so a clean regime split is not shown.

idea: Comparing whole harnesses cannot show which mechanism causes a gain; only controlled ablations can, and most papers lack them.
best_evidence: none: argued only, no ablation measured (2608.23653 page 13)
evidence_quality: weak: eight papers, authors state the limit about their own studies, no test of how often it misleads
why: Authors concede the limit in their own designs, but no paper measures how often whole-harness comparisons mislead. Argued only.

idea: Adding a memory system to a harness does not reliably beat the harness's own built-in memory, and the best added system differs by model.
best_evidence: Added memory scored lower than native memory in 11 of 50 cells, 8 of them under Hermes (2609.32391 page 8).
evidence_quality: medium: ten models and three harnesses, but single runs and the authors built the adapters.
why: Ten-model study plus a later paired null agree; nothing of equal date contradicts. Authors built adapters and ran once, so the gap sizes are soft.

idea: When a task needs information that outlives the context (analysis state, evidence state, workspace, lessons file), removing that external state costs points on strong models.
models: GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GLM-5.3
best_evidence: BixBench accuracy 79.02% to 56.59% without persistent memory (2609.03871, page not recorded); evidence state outside context 0.77 versus 0.60 pooled agreement (2610.40906).
evidence_quality: medium: many ablations on strong models, but all by the authors of the harness, mostly single runs.
why: Consistent ablations from September to November on strong models. Later nulls (2611.12552, 2611.19359) concern recaps and fixed shared notes, a different regime, see next idea. Cost effect can be time, not solved count (2611.04196).

idea: Memory that only repeats what the agent already saw, a recap of its last finding after compaction, or fixed shared notes without editing, adds no measurable success.
best_evidence: Recap after compaction 47 of 98 versus 48 of 98 resolved, minus 1.0 points [-8.3, +6.3] (2611.19359 page 4).
evidence_quality: medium: 98 paired tasks but one small model, one run per arm, no bare baseline, sign flipped between batches.
why: Two November nulls, one citing an earlier 11-of-12 null; none against. Power only for about 12-point effects, so small gains are not excluded.

idea: Generic frozen memory or experience add-ons on small models often score at or below the plain model; gains appear only for add-ons built for that task and executor.
best_evidence: ACE -8.2, Dynamic Cheatsheet -5.3, ExpeL -3.8 average change versus ReAct on Qwen3-8B (2608.05446); Mem0 19.5 versus 25.1 with no memory on Qwen3-32B (2605.30712).
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree, bare baselines present, but single runs and baselines wired by the authors.
why: Absorbs the first-pass idea that more components hurt small models. Newest papers agree; the one task-built rule system (2611.15268) helps, which fits the idea.

idea: Injecting a fixed library of past knowledge (plugins, past trials, recovery knowledge) adds no measurable gain once the harness or adaptive probing already works.
best_evidence: Probe-only 15 of 110 versus static knowledge 13 of 110, exact McNemar p = 0.79 (2610.27417 page not recorded); Kimi-K3 held-out 64.00% against 63.00% (2609.32423).
evidence_quality: medium: four nulls on different tasks and models; each small, single run, authors' own harness.
why: Four nulls on different setups; the only gain (2610.16625) was partly design-specific, distilled from the known designs. Gains seem to need knowledge matched to the target.

idea: Keeping complete unmodified interaction history is at least as good as reflection or rule extraction; reflection harnesses are less consistent than raw context and sometimes fall below the stateless model.
models: Kimi K3, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.7 Flash
best_evidence: Kimi K3 full history Max 63.3 versus 62.4 EvoTest and 61.6 Reflexion (2610.08215 page 6); GEPA-Online -0.134 on MemoryBench with Gemini 3.7 Flash (2610.12668 Table 1).
evidence_quality: medium: three papers agree, three trials or rollouts, gaps small, authors built the games.
why: Raw history is the baseline to beat. The same ReHarness paper shows revised notes beat top-k raw notes, so rewriting with outcome feedback may work; plain reflection does not.

idea: On repeated tasks keep concrete artifacts (demonstrations, programs, the previous controller, the workspace), not model-written prose; harnesses that persisted prose gained nothing over a demonstration cache.
models: Qwen3.5-9B, GLM-5.3 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5
best_evidence: Program library Sseen 0.65 and 0.81 while prime-agent persistence was -0.01 [-0.04, 0.03] (2611.14505 page 7); previous controller 7 of 8 versus 4 of 9 (2611.16867).
evidence_quality: medium: independent benchmark plus two supporting papers; one stream, one run per condition, small models.
why: Splits the first-pass idea on keeping state. Within a task family, raw artifacts carried forward help; prose lessons did not compound (2610.14495). Shipped harnesses kept none of the demonstrations they paid for.

idea: Carrying learned knowledge or harness edits to different tasks or domains: some papers show transfer, others show worse scores than resetting.
best_evidence: Keeping edits across tasks 78.33 versus 81.00 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 39.11 versus 44.44 on DeepSWE 1.1 when reset (2611.05139 Figure 4); transfer +8.54 average over 30 pairs, 7 negative (2610.39884).
evidence_quality: medium: both sides measured with baselines on strong models, but different tasks, single splits, authors' own systems.
why: Independent-looking November null and the reset result oppose transfer gains of Oct on stronger models; unvalidated carry-over loses, validated gated knowledge may transfer. Could not separate regimes from the notes.

idea: Failure-derived rules help most on tasks the model never solves and add nothing on tasks it mostly solves, where weights or the standard harness already do well.
best_evidence: Never-solved retail tasks: rules alone 44% versus weights alone 25%; always-solved 87% versus 95% (2611.15268 page 7); full conversations 82.9% versus 81.6% with lessons (2611.11342 page 3).
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, no bare run of the same model, never-solved set chosen after failure.
why: Replaces the contested first-pass idea by splitting regimes: rescue where the baseline fails, nothing where baseline success is already high. Selection effect on never-solved tasks is a caveat.

idea: Do not rely on the agent to write or read its own memory voluntarily; the harness must trigger writes and inject stored facts at fixed points such as every compaction.
best_evidence: 0 voluntary memory calls in 114 turns with a seeded store; harness injection delivered all facts at 138 of 138 compact-resumes (2607.20972 pages 5 and 8); 1 of 18 harnesses checkpoints (2609.01437).
evidence_quality: medium: direct counts in three papers on several models, but few runs and the injection system is the authors' own.
why: Three papers on small and strong models agree; one argued-style agent consolidation (2609.27302) is a single run description. Injection cost 36% more in one probe.

idea: Memory content steers the agent strongly, for good or ill: misleading guidance lowers frontier scores, poisoned memory keeps firing across sessions, and a stated preference shifts sources; validate and filter before reuse.
models: Claude Opus 5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
best_evidence: Bad guidance lowers frontier scores in all 12 model-task pairs by 2.3 to 43.3 points (2609.39578 page 5); poisoned rule 93.3 after five benign rounds in Claude Code (2609.13889).
evidence_quality: medium: several models, a placebo control and 3,000 trials in one paper; guidance benchmarks authored by the papers' makers.
why: Four independent-ish papers from September to November on strong models; none finds memory inert on a relevant effect (placebo memory had none, as expected).

idea: Stored entries go stale when the environment changes, and reusing them blind costs points; memory-based learners keep acting on stale memories after an unannounced rule change.
best_evidence: Blind reuse -5.3 points on average against +0.6 with recalibration (2607.26722); six of seven models score lower on day 2 after an environment change (2604.23781).
evidence_quality: weak: simulated settings, authored benchmarks, remedies measured only in June and July.
why: Harm of staleness is measured on strong models through November. The remedies (write-time invalidation, recalibration) rest on simulations and have no later replication, so only the harm is claimed.

idea: Memory has an optimum size: a small curated set beats none, but adding more stored statements stops helping and can hurt, and distilled banks matched full history with far less text.
best_evidence: Violations 0.77 with no memory, 0.20 at 10 statements, 0.25 to 0.27 at 20 to 150 (2609.36892 page 7); distilled bank 52.60% versus full 51.25% with 69.66% less text (2609.39284).
evidence_quality: medium: one model per paper, single numbers; but three independent September papers.
why: Replaces the stale first-pass idea on selective memory. Full history still wins when it fits (2611.06445 Full History 0.77 against summarizer 0.47), so the idea is about large stores.

idea: Structured memory (typed, hierarchical or commit-only records) beats flat raw history in the authors' ablations, but a rigorous raw-history baseline matched or beat reflection and compression.
best_evidence: Commit-only memory 57.81 full versus 44.74 without the memory operator, paired difference 13.07 [10.71, 15.43] (2610.05382); Full History 0.77 beat compressors on LongMemEval-S (2611.06445).
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own ablations on authored benchmarks; raw-history comparisons mostly on small or fitting histories.
why: Ablations favour structure, independent comparisons favour raw history; a split by whether history fits the window is plausible but unverified here.

idea: No single memory storage method wins everywhere; the best depends on the model and the capability tested, and a query router's gain vanished when held out by conversation.
best_evidence: Router 0.671 against 0.648 on random folds but 0.649 against 0.648 leaving one conversation out (2608.15008); no best system for every model (2609.32391 page 8).
evidence_quality: medium: ten-model grid plus a four-benchmark study; single greedy runs, small models in the second.
why: Two measurement studies agree and nothing contradicts. Test candidate memory designs on your own model and task rather than adopting a winner.

idea: A text working memory the model rewrites lifts frontier direct control sharply, but inside a policy harness it barely helps and visual replay hurts; code-only policies kept state better than agent harnesses.
best_evidence: Success 46.7% to 81.7% with text working memory; inside a policy harness 22.5% to 25.0% (2611.11509 pages 6 to 8).
evidence_quality: weak: one core model, simulator only, authors' own method; second paper compares against copied leaderboard numbers.
why: Measured on the strongest model with a bare baseline and nothing contradicts. Robot tasks, so transfer to coding is by analogy.

idea: Counting or tracking state across a long history stays weak even with memory tools: best counting score 47.58%, and no configuration produced a fully correct updated requirement state.
models: Muse Spark-1.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.7-Flash, Claude Opus 5.5
best_evidence: Exact post-state accuracy 0 of 312 for every configuration (2611.07307); best counting 47.58% (177 of 372) (2610.32332 page 7).
evidence_quality: medium: two benchmarks on many frontier models; authors' benchmarks, one run per condition.
why: Measured on frontier models in October and November, no contrary paper. Aggregation over history is a gap memory harnesses do not close.

idea: Judging a memory feature needs matched controls and repeated runs: rerunning an unchanged setup flipped about one task in five, and neutral or placebo arms explain apparent gains.
best_evidence: Same no-memory setup run twice changed outcome on 18.75% of tasks (2611.19359 page 3).
evidence_quality: medium: five recent papers agree, mostly small models and single streams.
why: Recent papers all show single-run gaps flip or vanish. No contrary measurement.

idea: Shared memory may pay off in speed and cost rather than solved count: removing it cost 2 solved cases of 40 but raised time to success 76.2%.
best_evidence: 28 solved without memory against 30, time to success +76.2% (2611.04196); far recall 69.9 versus 61.8 at 18.3 versus 42.1 dollars (2609.26891).
evidence_quality: weak: two papers, one task family each, authors' own systems, no repeats stated.
why: Thin evidence but nothing contradicts on time or cost. Measure time and cost, not just pass counts, when judging memory.

idea: File-backed state and handoff files let long runs resume and raise scores; measured only in March on one small model, other support is argued.
best_evidence: OSWorld 44.40 to 58.30 and SWE-bench Verified 73.00 to 75.60 with file-backed state (2603.25723).
evidence_quality: weak: one model, one measurement, rest are arguments.
why: Only measurement is March on a model later papers do not call strong, never re-tested. September findings on external state (above) point the same way but test other designs.

idea: Keeping full traces, not only scores, helps an automatic search for a better memory or retrieval harness.
best_evidence: Search-found retrieval harness +4.7 average, 34.1 to 38.8 over no retrieval (Table 6, page 9).
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own search, one run, held-out average includes the search model.
why: Direct measurement is July on weaker models. Later shared-library and reset results (2609.32423, 2611.05139) are not about traces, so not re-tested.

idea: Memory derived from low-trust inputs should inherit the lowest trust and be revocable; injected design documents did not stop an agent re-proposing an existing subsystem.
best_evidence: No measurement; 2609.05510 reports 3 consecutive sessions re-proposing an existing subsystem, argued.
evidence_quality: weak: argued designs and one anecdote, no measurements.
why: Arguments only. Related measured harm from poisoned memory is in an earlier idea.

idea: With a strong model, specialist roles, model-chosen delegation, parallel runs and peer broadcast add nothing measurable over one plain agent session at equal budget, and often cost more.
models: Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.5, GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4
best_evidence: GLM 5.2 medal rate: base 55.7, with delegation 45.2, with broadcast and three parallel runs 33.3 (2609.40303 page 7); FoamBench single Opus 4.6 96.4% against 88.2% specialized (2609.03718 page 5)
evidence_quality: medium: three September to October measurements on strong models, but single runs, wide intervals, authors favour the single design
why: Newest measurements agree and the contrary papers are June, with a weaker or author-built baseline. Large structured teams on decomposable work are a separate regime (see the team scaling idea).

idea: Model-chosen delegation to subagents works only on the strongest models; small or cheap models often never delegate, or score below the bare assistant, and delegation is the weakest skill across local models.
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Palmyra X6, qwen3.6-flash, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct
best_evidence: Delegation reliability: Palmyra X6 0.86, Sonnet 4.6 0.85, Flash 3.5 0.45, Qwen 3.6 0.42 (2607.06906 page 14); retrieval 86% against sub-agents 66% (2609.04898)
evidence_quality: medium: four papers agree, mostly mid-tier or small models, one run each, author-built tasks
why: Newest evidence is November on a small model. Harness-coded planner and workers worked on that same small model, so the floor concerns model-decided delegation, not decomposition itself.

idea: Whether the harness fixes the order of agent calls or a model orchestrates is unsettled: a fixed loop won on rule checking, a model orchestrator won on abstract puzzles, and only top models delegate well.
best_evidence: Fixed loop beat the model-ordered loop for all four models by 0.008 to 0.245 union accuracy (2607.25566 page 5); orchestrator 67.25% against pipeline 57.50% pass@2 (2607.06764 page 12)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, different tasks, single runs, no spread; the November benchmark confounds model and harness
why: Comparable-quality measurements point opposite ways on different tasks and no paper tested the choice directly. 2611.12856 adds that the best score was only 36.95% when models choose their own delegation.

idea: Parallel workers or explorers raise coverage quickly, then flatten near three to five workers, and duplicate moves grow with worker count; extra agents can lower accuracy on multiple-choice questions.
best_evidence: Coverage 33.2% at 1 worker, 52.5% at 3, 64.7% at 15, 62.7% at 20; duplicate moves 92.5% at 3 workers, 98.6% at 20 (ext-harness-engineering-small-language-models-explore pages 5-6)
evidence_quality: medium: five repeats on three datasets, but author-built benchmark and an underpowered matched-token test
why: Two independent tasks show saturation and GPQA fell from 78.0% at three agents to 74.0% at five (2607.27994). Structured teams with shared claims kept gaining to 128 agents (2609.26781), so this holds for unstructured sampling.

idea: A separate critic or auditor role that sees the task and the changes lifts coding and retrieval agents at modest cost; more critics add a little; self-review and scripted reflection add nothing.
best_evidence: Four independent critics beat one critic by 3.1 points on Terminal-Bench at 1.33 times total cost (2610.34577 pages 8-9); removing review roles 53.45 to 48.82 (2610.33106)
evidence_quality: medium: seven strong models, three trials in the main paper, but several authors' own systems and no variance reported
why: Many October measurements on several models support it. Null results are a different structure: a one-shot read matched a pipeline (2611.00420) and a staged harness tied a plain tool loop (2609.13005).

idea: Subagents with a specific task and their own tool access help; generic lifecycle subagents and advisory subagents that only recommend actions do not.
models: Qwen3.7-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 5
best_evidence: Task-specific subagents +5.91 points on Qwen3.7-Max ProgramBench (2609.32459 page 9); acting subagents beat advisory ones by +0.26 on critical actions (2609.13543 page 9)
evidence_quality: medium: four papers across coding, clinical and interface tasks, but each one benchmark, one run, some synthetic
why: Consistent across domains with newest evidence in October; native generic subagents also cost accuracy and money on long coding tasks (2606.10662). Small samples, so gain size is uncertain.

idea: Adding specialist agents or loosely coupled components to a working system can lose earlier abilities or fall below the better component, so rerun old tasks after each addition.
best_evidence: Backward transfer -34.7% when specialist agents were added, against -5.3% for tools and -4.0% for skills (2609.04280 page 11); combination below its better component on 13 of 26 tasks (2610.35832 page 20)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own benchmarks, repeats unstated, and one robot case is not a software harness
why: Measured September and October on frontier models and nothing contradicts it. Quality stays weak because both benchmarks are the authors' own.

idea: Subagents that inherit the parent's expensive model multiply cost; routing them to a cheaper tier saves money, but quality under routing was never measured.
best_evidence: Five subagents cost $5.09 on Fable 5.1 and $1.32 on Sonnet 5 (2609.28919 page 9)
evidence_quality: weak: simulated bills on authors' synthetic conversations, list prices, no live run, no quality measure
why: Price arithmetic and a simulation, not a measured result; the same paper found false downgrades in moved turns, so savings may cost quality.

idea: Mixing the work of structurally different harnesses (merged specialists, a shared blackboard) solves more than the best single harness; measured only before September on one-run, selection-style counts.
best_evidence: Merged harness 28 of 41 held-out tasks against specialists 24, 25, 26, 27 (2608.07545 page 13); blackboard 19/33, union 17/33, best single 15/33 (2605.28334)
evidence_quality: weak: one run each, author wrappers, union counts act as an oracle, no bare baseline
why: Four pre-September gains versus a September null where broadcast between parallel runs of one harness scored 33.3 against 55.7 for a plain session. Tasks differ, nobody re-tested the blackboard, so unresolved.

idea: A parent that spawns a full agent harness per document entry in parallel beat a published coding-agent score on long-context aggregation with the same model.
best_evidence: 81.36% against 71.75% for a published Codex score, 199 tasks (2606.13643 page 4)
evidence_quality: weak: baseline is another paper's number, no ablation, no bare run, one benchmark
why: Measured only in June on GPT-5 and never re-tested; the paper ran no ablations, so recursion depth and spawning are untested.

idea: Roles that keep isolated contexts and exchange only pass or fail messages beat an orchestrator that shares planning context.
best_evidence: 67.4% against 61.1% on SWE-bench Pro, 731 tasks (2606.25514 page 16)
evidence_quality: weak: orchestrator baseline built by the authors, one run, no bare-model baseline
why: Only June evidence; later studies show extra structure adding nothing on strong models and none re-tested message isolation. The October single-committer finding (2610.05382) is a different mechanism.

idea: A cheap or small model inside a fixed multi-role loop with scripted checks can match or beat a much stronger bare model on narrow structured tasks; first versions of such loops can fail badly.
best_evidence: Haiku full pipeline 0.948 against Opus zero-shot 0.806 (2610.19999 page 7); DeepSeek-v4-flash 0.9542 against GPT-5.5 0.9759 at $1.1969 against $4.5860 (2607.25566 pages 7-8)
evidence_quality: medium: papers from July to November, but author-built benchmarks, single runs, and pipeline also adds state and tools
why: Newest evidence November. Floor exists: a 7B model scored 3% against 30% zero-shot in its first version (2611.12079) and only repaired versions helped; the cause inside the pipeline is not isolated.

idea: Giving one agent the whole tool or skill catalog does not reliably help: it raised errors in one paper but raised pass rate at higher token cost in another.
best_evidence: Single agent with 47 tools failed integrity checks on 21 of 459 runs against 7 of 459 zero-shot (2610.19999 page 9); full catalog 30.2% against 26.0% but 75.8M against 27.2M tokens (2609.04280 page 7)
evidence_quality: weak: one run each, author-built tasks, different task types and models
why: Measurements of similar date point both ways on different tasks and models; no regime split is supported by the evidence.

idea: Multi-agent and harness effects differ in sign by model and task, so pooled averages hide losses; report gained and lost cases per model against the bare call.
models: Claude Opus 4.6, Llama 4 Maverick, Qwen3.7-Max, MiniMax-M2.5
best_evidence: After-edit reminder +14.3 on Qwen3.7-Max, -3.6 on MiniMax-M2.5 (2610.34577 page 5); map-reduce on sycophancy: Opus 4.6 -16.8 points, Llama 4 Maverick +18.8 (2603.10044 page 31)
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, one run or three trials each, pooled numbers shown to mislead
why: Five papers, newest November, show per-model reversals and none contradicts: workflows written by Opus 5.5 helped weaker executors, those written by GPT-6 Astra averaged -2.53. Test every change per model.

idea: Automatically evolved or refined multi-agent harnesses beat fixed hand-built protocols mostly on tasks close to their tuning set; gains often come from prompt wording and one added tool, not new coordination.
best_evidence: Optimized multi-agent 71.88 against unoptimized 67.27 and best single agent 68.69; prompt-only optimization fell to 64.62 (2611.15754 page 3)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own loops, small tuning sets, no held-out tasks in several, language-model judges
why: Replaces the first-pass user-written-workflow idea. Gains reported by many authors, but November papers show prompt-only edits losing, ties against integrated search and degrading alternating updates; regimes not separable from the evidence.

idea: On long decomposable tasks, many parallel agents sharing an append-only typed record, exclusive task claims and one workspace raise score and speed; a single agent never reached the same level.
best_evidence: Pandoc test-pass rate 33.89% with 1 agent, 50.94% with 128, 55.06% with 1,024 (2609.26781 page 6); 93.33% against 81.67% for Claude Code on Opus 5.5 (2606.10662 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, one model in the large study, five tasks, no bare model run, repeats unstated
why: Newest support is September on the strongest models with a shared-state design. A September null on single-answer machine learning tasks (2609.40303) fits a regime difference: decomposable work against one answer.

idea: Parallel agents that talk freely or only know a peer exists collide on interacting work: success collapses, awareness does not fix it, and larger peer groups do worse than pairs.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V4 Flash
best_evidence: Opus 4.8 success on contradictory tasks fell from 62% for one agent to 16% for parallel agents (2611.00314 page 8); peer awareness 16% to 26%, not significant (2611.00314 page 9)
evidence_quality: medium: 155 and 488 scenarios across several models, but author-built, repeats not stated, one table partly unverified
why: Three independent studies in September and October agree and the structured shared-state teams of the scaling idea avoid the problem. Sequential hand-off recovered part of the loss (16% to 54%).

idea: Subagents and extra roles raise cost, roughly 1.1 to 1.5 times in measured cases; buy the cost only where a measured gain pays for it.
best_evidence: Claude Code with subagents 80.00% accuracy at $30.88 per task against 81.67% at $20.31 without (2606.10662 page 8); critics 1.33 times cost (2610.34577)
evidence_quality: medium: cost reported in several papers on strong models, but small task counts and cost accounting differs
why: Costs rose in every measured case and some added nothing in accuracy. Subagent price arithmetic alone is the unmeasured routing idea.

idea: Delegation widens the safety and permission surface: multi-agent setups lowered tool adherence, per-agent capability scopes blocked injected effects that one shared policy let through, and subagents reused approvals unless blocked.
best_evidence: Tool adherence 0.91 single against 0.64 multi-agent (2605.14271 page 10); injected effects passed in 3/75 with per-agent scopes against 33/75 with one task policy (2609.08371 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: author benchmarks, offline replay, frameworks differ in more than role count, older or mid models
why: Four measurements through November agree on enforcement at each subagent; the March null concerned answer safety, not permissions. Treat as a design requirement, not an effect size.

idea: Information is lost at parent to child handoffs and in combined approval replies; pass exact artifacts or shared records, not a summary the parent writes.
best_evidence: Information handoff recall 0.322 on Live-SWE and 0.553 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 against 1.00 for direct prompting (2603.25723 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: one small model in the handoff study; three tasks in the framework study
why: Two measurements, March and November, on different frameworks and models agree and none disagrees. Few tasks, so a warning to test handoffs rather than a size estimate.

idea: A multi-stage or multi-agent pipeline taken from another paper, or built without tuning, often scores below the bare model or the best single agent; the gain belongs to a tuned design.
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5
best_evidence: Every reproduced multi-stage story system scored 7.2 to 37.7 points below its zero-shot base model (2609.15188 page 8); unoptimized multi-agent 67.27 against best single agent 68.69 (2611.15754)
evidence_quality: medium: four base models and several tasks, but reproduced baselines may be weakly tuned
why: Four September to November measurements on strong models agree and none contradicts. The same paper's own tuned harness beat zero-shot on all four models, so tuning separates win from loss.

idea: A strong model that writes the workflow for weaker executor models can lift them, but the sign depends on which model authors it.
models: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GPT-6 Luna
best_evidence: Opus 5.5 workflows added 6.41 points on average with static transfer across four weaker executors; GPT-6 Astra workflows averaged -2.53 (2611.12856 page 11)
evidence_quality: weak: one run per configuration, benchmark by the authors, model and harness effects confounded
why: Newest evidence November on the strongest models, one benchmark and no contradiction. Pairing a trained interface coder with other reasoning models also helped in October (2610.11123).

idea: A routed set of cheaper proposer models with an aggregator can match the strongest single model at about one third the cost; adding more judges gives small, flattening gains.
best_evidence: Routed ensemble 60.82 at $0.3766 against Fable 5 59.80 at $1.2122 per task (2607.11399 page 17); judge reject score 0.81 at one judge to 0.86 at seven (2608.09857)
evidence_quality: weak: one benchmark, authors' own routing, one-point margin, no repeats reported
why: Measured on models still strong in later papers and nothing newer tests it, but the margin is one point and a diverse-agent ensemble lost accuracy on multiple-choice questions in July (2607.27994).

idea: No single harness wins everywhere: the best harness changes with the model and the benchmark, and a model's rank can reverse under another harness, so test model and harness as a pair.
models: Qwen3.8 Max, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol, GLM-5.3
best_evidence: Harness gap between OpenHands and OpenCode runs from minus 9.05 to plus 11.90 points; GLM-5.3 scores 40.00% against 49.05% (2611.14952 page 6).
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree on strong models, newest has three runs, but no bare-model baseline and authors built the benchmarks.
why: Seven papers from June to November agree, the newest on five strong models. No measurement finds one harness leading everywhere, so choose the harness per model and task.

idea: Vendor-built harnesses do not reliably beat neutral or minimal harnesses on the same model; some help their own model, some hurt it.
models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-sol, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5
best_evidence: Opus 4.8 scores 54.0 under Pi and 66.2 under Claude Code, while GPT-5.6-sol falls from 52.9 to 26.2 under Codex (2610.28679 page 6, Table 3).
evidence_quality: medium: same models in two harnesses, but authors built tasks, runs are few, and vendors train models on their own harness.
why: Same-quality studies disagree even on one model family: Codex leads for GPT-5.6-sol in one paper and trails Pi in another. Vendor training and task type may explain it, but no paper separates them.

idea: A harness a model evolves for itself reaches about the level of strong production harnesses on the newest models but not above it; grown from a near-empty seed it trails the human-built one clearly.
models: GLM-5.3, GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5
best_evidence: Evolved versus production harness: GLM-5.3 59.01 against 58.88, GPT-5.6 Sol 60.64 against 59.56, intervals include zero (2609.38372 page 9).
evidence_quality: medium: four papers agree on strong models, but each is the authors' own system, mostly single runs, no bare baseline.
why: Parity on top models in September and November; the best self-built harness scored 67.8 against 86.2 for the human one. Two contrary papers search with outside proposers and win by one or two points on the tuned benchmark.

idea: A harness that edits itself or is searched gains only when every edit is checked on held-out tasks before it is kept; edits accepted unchecked can lower scores.
best_evidence: Self-evolution without verification never beat the start harness on validation; with verification test 41.05% against 39.81% (2610.02616 Table 1, page 4).
evidence_quality: weak: most rows are one evolution run, authors' own benchmarks, reimplemented baselines, validation also shapes the edits.
why: Three papers with a validation or generalization gate report gains, while the one paper with no gate saw GPT-5.6 Luna lose 9.23 points. No paper finds unchecked edits safe.

idea: Harness gains measured on the tasks used to tune the harness overstate what holds on unseen tasks: the held-out gain is smaller or absent.
models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5
best_evidence: Second revision gains 8.42 points on development games but 2.80 held-out, interval minus 1.44 to plus 7.35 (2610.30499 page 6).
evidence_quality: medium: five papers use held-out splits, but single or few runs and authors' own benchmarks.
why: Papers that separate tuning from held-out tasks find the smaller gain, newest late October on strong models. Three papers (one in October) show clear positive transfer, so the held-out gain is smaller, not always absent.

idea: A harness tuned on one model often fails to carry over unchanged to another model, but harnesses that carry task knowledge such as notes, rules or abstention logic often do carry over.
models: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Kimi K3
best_evidence: A harness evolved on GPT-5.6-Luna gained 6.7 to 40.0 points on abstention across 19 other models (2610.06563 page 7).
evidence_quality: medium: many papers on both sides, all authors' own systems, mostly single runs, no bare baselines.
why: Papers of equal date disagree: one transfers to 19 models, another finds zero-shot transfer near zero, and a harness for an earlier version of a model lowered a later version by 17 points. Task type may explain it, untested.

idea: The gain from adding tools or a task harness shrinks as the model gets stronger, on tasks the weaker model can already partly do.
models: Claude Opus 5, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, Gemini-3.8-Flash
best_evidence: EvoX advantage over the other five harnesses: plus 10.7 with GLM-5.3, plus 0.4 with Opus 5 (2611.15006 page 10).
evidence_quality: weak: one run per cell, tasks not random, authors' own harness; second paper has two backbones and no repeats.
why: Newest two papers agree, and a learning-harness study found damage on tasks that needed no learning. Contrary cases are an earlier paper where stronger models gained more and a task the model could not do at all.

idea: On tasks the bare model almost never solves, a harness that supplies what the model lacks (images, notes, memory, tools) multiplies scores, even for the strongest models.
models: GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, GLM-5.3 Flash 320B
best_evidence: GPT-5.6 Sol on ARC-AGI-3: official baseline 13.33, full harness ladder 99.00 (2610.02200 page 6).
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, unequal budgets (part of the gain is larger limits), repeats not stated, tuned on public games.
why: Seven papers show multiples on tasks the bare model fails, on the strongest models in September and October. Limit: precise contact control and unseen composite tasks stayed unsolved, and a model-built harness scored 39.95 against 100.

idea: A harness fitted by its authors to their own task beats a bare or minimal loop on the same model, but published general harnesses do not reliably beat a minimal one.
best_evidence: Generated task harness improved all 18 matched model and benchmark pairs; GLM-5.2 average 74.1 to 81.8 (2608.25593 page 7).
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own harnesses tuned on the same benchmarks, mostly no repeats, mostly no bare-model run.
why: Fitted harnesses beat plain loops in eight papers up to November; the three contrary papers test harnesses built by others and find no reliable win over a single plain session. Wins sit mostly on tuned tasks.
