why: Three papers through 2026-11-02 agree with none against; evolved safety harnesses lower attack success on tested attacks yet raised unsafe outcomes on unseen scenarios (17.00% static against a higher evolving rate).

idea: Evolution that uses no ground-truth labels, only the agent's own runs or unlabeled test inputs, still raises held-out scores, so a harness can adapt at deployment.
best_evidence: BIRD execution accuracy 12.7% to 48.7%, mean of three runs, with evolution on each unlabeled batch (2607.08124)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own systems, mostly single benchmarks; one autonomous-accumulation null on molecular workflows
why: Six papers through 2026-11-11 report label-free gains; one 2026-10-27 study found no held-out gain and a final checkpoint below baseline, so keep a validation gate even without labels.

idea: The same harness scores several points differently on repeated runs, so a gain under about five points on tens of tasks cannot be told from noise; repeat runs and report intervals.
best_evidence: The same commit varies by about 4.75 points across runs (2609.01437 page 13)
evidence_quality: medium: six papers report spreads or intervals; numbers come from authors' benchmarks with few repeats
why: Six papers to 2026-11-09 report run spread of several points or intervals around zero for gains of two to five points; no paper shows otherwise.

idea: Task-matched expert knowledge placed in context (domain tutorials, method rules, procedural skills) lifts success sharply when the model lacks that knowledge, such as a new method or niche format.
models: Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Pro [max]
best_evidence: None of 20 bare phonon workflows used the grid rules correctly; all 10 with the knowledge layer did (2610.20779 page 7).
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree, large effects, but authors wrote both tasks and knowledge, and repeats are few
why: Many independent domains show big gains where the model lacks the knowledge; newest measurements in October and November on top models still agree. The gain is bounded to knowledge the model really lacks.

idea: Where the knowledge is already in the model, the gain from a task-matched reference shrinks as the model gets stronger: large for a weaker model, near zero for the strongest.
models: GPT-5.6 Sol [max], DeepSeek V4 Pro [max], GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8
best_evidence: Reference topology adds 18.7 points for DeepSeek V4 Pro but 0.7 for GPT-5.6 Sol at six hours (2609.33356 page 7).
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree in direction, but each author-built, mostly single runs, and strength is confounded with vendor
why: The newest same-library test (2610.35616) shows GLM-5.2 gaining more than GPT-5.5 or Opus 4.8. The October knowledge-layer paper shows full gains for every strength, so the idea holds only for known material.

idea: General skill libraries and broad guidance documents add little over a bare strong model; only content matched to the task moves results.
models: DeepSeek V4 Pro [max], GPT-5.5, GPT-5, Qwen3.8-27B
best_evidence: Three general skill formats finished within 3.3 points of the no-skill baseline at six hours (2609.33356 page 7).
evidence_quality: medium: five measurements agree on strong models, though tasks are author-built and repeats few
why: Newest measurements of general libraries (October) still show flat or small gains. The one larger gain (published skills, 4.6 to 19.5 points) used task-specific skills with a request to consult them.

idea: Skills distilled from trajectories of the same task family give frontier models modest held-out gains of a few points, and weaker models more; the gain survives a change of runtime.
best_evidence: A frozen library gave GPT-5.5 DeepSWE 67.2 to 73.5 and Opus 4.8 59.3 to 61.1 (2610.35616 page 9).
evidence_quality: medium: three runs, two runtimes, three models, held-out benchmark, but authors' own method and no spread on ablations
why: Newest and strongest-model measurement is positive with a no-skill baseline. Against it: a skill-only evolution that lowered reward in September, and a weaker solver that lost points in August.

idea: Lessons or rules distilled from a small model's own failures lift it on tasks like those it learned on, but whether they carry to unseen tasks or a stronger model is disputed.
models: Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.5-9B, Claude Sonnet 5, GLM-5.3 Flash
best_evidence: Held-out rule: airline pass1 56.0 to 75.5 for Gemma 4 12B (2611.15268 page 7); a lesson gain did not replicate, +0.31 held-out (2611.11342 page 3).
evidence_quality: medium: both sides are November, small models, authors' own setups, one run per condition
why: Papers a week apart disagree on held-out transfer; the difference is not clear (rules in context, editor equals agent, scorer defects in one benchmark). A neutral note matched lessons in one study.

idea: Wrong or misleading guidance costs more than none, and following guidance that has turned bad does worse than stopping it; reused retrieved skills can also score below no skill.
models: Gemini 3.7 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.2
best_evidence: Misleading workflows lowered scores by 2.3 to 43.3 points on four benchmarks for every frontier model (2609.39578 page 5).
evidence_quality: medium: twelve model-task pairs with a bare baseline, but single numbers and authors built the benchmarks
why: Two September papers and one July paper agree; nothing later contradicts. Skills must be checked as content, not trusted for being skills.

idea: Average success hides regressions: skills help some tasks and break tasks the bare model solved, so report paired gains and losses per task, not mean success alone.
best_evidence: The same Skills helped one pair and hurt another on 32 of 87 tasks, 36.78 percent (2610.08875 page 1).
evidence_quality: medium: four papers, paired designs, three runs per condition in the newest, authors built subsets
why: The first pass rated this stale from July only. Two October papers on newer models (GPT-5.5, GPT-6-Astra) show paired losses beside gains, so it is now re-tested and standing.

idea: Whether offered skills get loaded depends mainly on the model and on how they are offered: weak models and always-on listings rarely load them; preloading, path gating, routing or must-read wording raises loading.
models: GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Haiku 4.5
best_evidence: Always-on skills were opened in 0 of 198 rollouts, path-gated skills in 28 of 66 (2610.14216 page 31).
evidence_quality: medium: six papers agree across models and runtimes, but several use author-built benchmarks and few repeats
why: Consistent from May to October across eight or more models. Do not credit skills until load rate is measured.

idea: Loading a skill is not following it: models that load a skill still break requirements it states, and a skill helps completion only when its procedure is followed well.
models: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Claude Opus 4.8
best_evidence: Claude Opus 4.7 triggered 0.966 but complied 0.609; DeepSeek-V4-Pro 0.324 and 0.439 (2608.04828 page 6).
evidence_quality: medium: four papers agree; two benchmarks are author-built and one uses model judges, repeats not stated
why: Triggering and compliance are separate; even with all policies in context the best model violated about 30 percent. Measure adherence, not just presence.

idea: Rules the agent must obey every time belong in the prompt text; splitting a policy into skills loaded on demand costs accuracy for small models.
best_evidence: Airline pass1 56.0 with the policy split into skills against 67.5 with the full policy in the prompt (2611.15268 page 8).
evidence_quality: weak: one small model, one domain, the split had a known defect, no run without policy text
why: One November measurement plus a consolidation gain in October (55.7 to 64.4) agree; nothing contradicts. Low weight because of single model and the defect.

idea: One short, positive, factual sentence (verify the work, report the retrieval status, state a rejection, answer from the printed report) reliably changes a measurable behaviour; in the system message it beats the user message.
best_evidence: One appended sentence cut the dishonest rate from 14.10 to 0.87 percent (2609.14758 page 8); system-role verification +3.3 and +3.9 points (2610.34577 page 5).
evidence_quality: medium: tight effects on narrow behaviours, large samples in the status-line paper; coding gains small, three trials, no tests
why: Several independent papers from August to October agree on state or format statements. Limit: computed or history-dependent rules were not fixed by stating them (2609.36892).

idea: Prompt lines that forbid a behaviour, demand terse output, or name a preferred tool do not change what the model does; removing the alternative or adding a blocking gate does.
best_evidence: A terse-output instruction solved 2 to 5 fewer kernels per setup (2610.20673 page 6); do-not-repeat changed repeat likelihood by +0.07 nats (2608.23651 page 10).
evidence_quality: weak: tiny models with synthetic failures, thin repeats, one prose-only claim, no strong model
why: One narrow sentence of efficiency wording did hold on six models in August, so the limit is prohibitions and tool preferences, not all wording. Newest evidence is October.

idea: Telling the agent the reviewer's rules raises joint success but lowers plain functional success on every tested model, a trade the harness must price.
best_evidence: Joint success 41.3 to 52.8 for GPT-5.5, functional success down 0.7 points (2609.04167 page 6).
evidence_quality: weak: single paper, one benchmark, no repeats stated
why: Single September paper on a top model; nothing contradicts it. It matters for designs with outside reviewers but needs a second measurement.

idea: Against a minimal prompt, a general engineered prompt (role priming, a category checklist) lifts every model, most for the weakest; no strong model lost.
evidence_quality: medium: four models and a minimal baseline, but one task family and no repeats in the table
why: Replaces the contested first-pass claim about prompt length. Papers that found no gain or a loss used a tuned shipped prompt or older models, which splits the regimes.

idea: Added instructions over a vendor's tuned default prompt or a stronger harness give no gain and can hurt, for example security prompts over the shipped Codex prompt.
best_evidence: Codex default scored 70 and 70; security-specific prompts 64 and 58 and 60 and 68 (2607.13085 page 5).
evidence_quality: weak: one or two runs, authors build the benchmarks, the Opus 5 result rests on one run and one model
why: The October paper (Opus 5, one run) points the same way as July. The apparent clash with the engineered-prompt gain is a different baseline, minimal against tuned.

idea: The same skill or instruction can help one model or runtime and hurt another, so each pairing must be tested bare and with the skill; a skill written for one student also helps others less.
best_evidence: Detect score +22.8 percent for GPT-5.5 in Codex but -5.9 to -9.4 percent for DeepSeek-V4-Pro (2609.29454 page 7-8).
evidence_quality: medium: six papers agree in sign, mostly few runs; one finds 34 of 36 transfers improve
why: Newest papers (October, November) still show sign flips by model or harness. Skills optimised on one model transferred in 34 of 36 cases in September, so cross-model transfer is a possible but not safe default.

idea: Automated search that edits only prompts or skills gains a few points over a good seed; searching the whole harness (tools, memory, control code) gains more.
best_evidence: Prompt or skill only search gained at most +6.6 percent resolution on PaperBench (2609.38349 page 11).
evidence_quality: medium: compared with many harnesses, but authors' own systems and single searches
why: Newest direct comparison (November, +3.0 from a better prompt) and September papers agree. One vision-task paper found instruction refinement gave most of its gain, so the rule is for agent tasks.

idea: Skills and lessons built from grounded feedback (verifier output, test failures, a teacher's contrast with its own run) beat self-judged or human-written ones.
models: Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4 high, Claude-Sonnet-5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash
best_evidence: Self-generated feedback scored 27.96, below no evolution 29.54; verifier feedback 34.02 (2608.15071 page 8).
evidence_quality: medium: four papers, three different models, authors' own methods, repeats mostly not stated
why: Newest paper (November) agrees with August and May. Gains are modest and need a no-update baseline.

idea: A stronger model rewriting or adapting skills to fit a weak executor beats giving the weak model the generic skill or bank directly.
best_evidence: Builder-held meta-skills scored 65.31 against 53.29 for direct delivery (2609.38143 page 6).
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree, small to moderate gains, authors' own methods
why: Consistent from September to November. Fits small-model harnesses: write skills per executor.

idea: Skills organised as ordered stages with named artifact handoffs beat flat piles of atomic skills.
best_evidence: Seven-stage workflow added 7.3 points over the same atomic skills, 12 of 15 paired tasks won (2610.31158 page 24).
evidence_quality: weak: two papers, small subsets, authors' design
why: Two October papers agree; nothing contradicts. Small subsets and author-built tasks keep the weight low.

idea: Skill text is an attack surface and a safety lever: unvetted or poisoned skills raise violation rates, while a safety skill for the domain lowers them.
models: Kimi-K3, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6
best_evidence: Skill prose plus payload gave 38.0 percent attack success with Kimi-K3 in Codex, 0.0 payload-free (2609.35912 page 9).
evidence_quality: weak: authors build attacks, single runs, safety tasks designed to elicit failures
why: Reworded from the first pass (domain skills raise unsafe actions, stale). A September paper on twelve models shows removing a safety skill lowers a safety score, so both directions stand.

idea: Differences between agent runtimes shrink when the time budget or the scaffolding grows; the runtime matters most on an unscaffolded or short run.
best_evidence: Runtime spread 56.0 to 72.0 percent at two hours, 80.0 to 86.0 at six (2609.33356 page 7).
evidence_quality: weak: author-built tasks, one run per task in the runtime study, no intervals
why: Replaces the April claim. A September study on top models shows the gap narrowing with time. A skill-revision study shows runtime still flips the sign for one model.

idea: Merely listing a skill can change results even if its body is never read: description-only presence produced gains and regressions without any invocation.
best_evidence: 70 of 243 SpreadsheetBench regressions were osmosis, with invocation-free gains in the hundreds (2607.22520 page 5).
evidence_quality: weak: one paper with one run per condition and one coder labelling mechanisms
why: Measured once in July on models later papers no longer treat as strong; the June renaming test points the same way but was never re-tested.

idea: The same harness can lift one small model and hurt another of similar size, so test every small model with and without the harness.
best_evidence: Meno-Lite-0.1 rose 0.359 to 0.641 while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fell 0.691 to 0.497 under one harness (2609.34366 p4)
evidence_quality: medium: seven papers on different tasks show sign flips, but authors' own benchmarks and mostly single runs
why: Seven papers, newest November 2026, find harness effects flip sign between small models. No paper finds one harness helping every small model. Format validity as the cause is only argued.

idea: A harness built for small local models, with fixed control code such as recovery of cut-off replies, finish gates and accept-only-if-better, lifts them from near zero to usable.
best_evidence: Qwen3.8-27B perfect matches 37.5% (24/64) to 100% (64/64) from bare to full harness (ext-agentic-pcg-harness-controlled-local-models p6)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree and one has a bare baseline, but authors' own benchmarks, single runs, prompt mixed with harness
why: Newest measurements are from September to November 2026 and nothing later reverses them. Dissent is a flat Gemma4:e2B near ceiling and two 8B models at zero with or without a harness. Single parts can hurt alone.

idea: Off-the-shelf general agent harnesses fail on models of about four billion parameters or fewer, so the harness must be sized to the model; below about 3 billion generic loops and teaching add nothing.
best_evidence: On gemma4:e2b opencode scored 0.017 and goose 0.271 against 0.821 for the purpose-built harness (2610.02001 p16)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers agree across models, but authors' own harnesses, one run per cell, mostly no bare model run
why: Newest papers (October and November 2026) show stock loops at zero or flat on 1.7B to 4B models, while a 27B model mostly completed in 2608.08654. Tailored harnesses on the same sizes work, so the floor applies to generic ones.

idea: A tuned harness lets a small or cheap model reach most of a frontier model's accuracy at a fraction of the cost, on narrow and repetitive task families.
best_evidence: DeepSeek-v4-flash 0.9542 against 0.9759 for GPT-5.5 at $1.1969 against $4.5860 per scenario (2607.25566 p7-8)
evidence_quality: medium: many papers agree, but authors built their own task suites and bare baselines are mostly missing
why: Newest result is November 2026. Gains shrink on hard or diverse tasks: a 35B coordinator reached 23.7% against 70.0% for the frontier model in 2610.24744, and Haiku 4.5 could not finish hard theorems in 2605.26959.

idea: Automatic harness search or evolution lifts some small models close to frontier accuracy but gives nothing or loses on others, so the lift is not predictable from model size.
best_evidence: qwen3-coder-30b-a3b-instruct 29.2% to 78.0% (2609.09134 p4) against GPT-5nano BFCL lift -24.7 (2609.05736 p12)
evidence_quality: medium: measured on both sides with repeats in places, but all authors' own benchmarks and no bare baselines
why: Qwen3.5-9B ALFWorld rose 53.0 to 97.0 while three small models with plans at 0.13 to 0.17 stayed within noise and gpt-5-mini showed no gain. Tasks and optimizers differ; I could not split by competence alone.

idea: More structure, more feedback, more stacked features or a generic hint can make a weaker model worse, so add each part and test it on the small model itself.
best_evidence: GPT-OSS-120B-Q4KM fell 0.4754 to 0.1719 when full feedback went into one prompt (2607.25566 p5)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers on different tasks agree, but authors' own benchmarks and mostly single runs
why: Papers show a weaker model losing from added feedback, a generic hint, stacked features or a stricter template; gpt-5.4-nano passed 15 then 12 of 89 after stacking. Newest is October 2026 and nothing shows the reverse.

idea: Training a 4B to 9B model on traces produced inside the harness it will run in beats prompting it, and on some tasks beat larger or frontier models.
best_evidence: Trained 4B scored Pass@3 58.00 against 46.67 for Claude Opus 5 in the same harness (2610.11123 p3)
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own benchmarks, partly in-domain test sets, mostly no repeats, comparison favours the trained model
why: Many papers on web, robot, vision and terminal tasks agree and the newest is October 2026. Untrained 4B models stay weak in the same harness. Fixed-harness fine-tuning can cost general instruction following (2608.15763).

idea: Copying a stronger model's full trajectories can hurt or install nothing in a small model; on-policy correction or reinforcement is safer, though other papers gain a lot from plain trace training.
best_evidence: Imitation under the evolved harness 78.0% to 63.1% across all seven tasks (2609.09134 p4)
evidence_quality: weak: three papers on one side, different tasks, one paper with three runs, small correction gain within noise
why: At 4B supervised imitation was rejected in all three updates (2610.10426) while reinforcement moved 67 to 79 tasks, yet Qwen3.5-4B gained 22.6 to 44.8 from supervised training on rollouts (2610.26071). Teacher strength and data filtering may explain it.

idea: Expert-written knowledge, playbooks or notes with deterministic command-line tools, written once by a strong model or expert, lets open-weight models reach full marks on specialist tasks they fail bare.
best_evidence: Every agent reached maximum GW and GW-BSE scores with the layer against 53.6% and 36.0% bare averages (2610.20779 p5)
evidence_quality: weak: authors wrote skills and rubrics for the same few tasks; mostly single runs; Qwen3.8-27B still trails on tables
why: Six papers, newest November 2026, show knowledge written by a strong source lifting weaker models, including Gemini 3.8 Flash 23.8% to 53.8% (2611.11509). The 1.7B student gained nothing; this fits proprietary frameworks but tasks are tuned.

idea: Small models often skip or drop self-evolved skills, and a full skill library can lower success, so check skill loading and adherence first.
best_evidence: Skill load rate 0.251 for Qwen3-32B and 0.446 for GPT-OSS-120B against 0.957 to 0.961 for stronger models (2605.30621 p8)
evidence_quality: weak: unvalidated model judge, no repeats on main benchmarks, 14B gap of 4 points is noise
why: Measured only before September 2026 on older Qwen models. Later expert skills with deterministic tools worked on small models, a different design, so the loading problem is untested on current models.

idea: A small model used as controller to decide when a stronger agent stops or verifies raises cost without raising the pass rate.
best_evidence: Small model controller cost 1.47 times native with 76.2% against 73.0% pass (2610.24649 p3)
evidence_quality: weak: one paper, 21 tasks, pass intervals about plus or minus 11 to 13 points
why: One recent paper with a bare baseline, equal budgets and a random-advice placebo that matched the pass rate for less cost. Nothing contradicts it, but it is a single small study.

idea: Harness design, not the model or the tool interface, sets the token bill: the same model and task vary by large factors across harnesses, and fixed control code cuts model calls.
best_evidence: qwen3.6:27b used 17,416 to 2,418,828 tokens across harnesses, 139 times (2608.08654 p18)
evidence_quality: medium: one controlled seven-harness comparison plus authors' own systems that report the same direction
why: Four papers, newest September 2026, report large cost gaps from harness choice alone. The controlled study had one task and one run per hosted configuration.

idea: On question answering over files with a capable self-hosted open model, a near-empty file-tool harness lands within about one point of a large production harness.
best_evidence: 83.8% for the near-empty harness against 85.0% for the bare Claude Code SDK (2611.03434 p2)
evidence_quality: weak: one model, a three-question gap, no repeats, authors' company benchmark
why: Newest result is November 2026. Terminal tasks still showed gains in 2611.05139, so I limited the claim to file question answering where the bare model already passes most tasks.

idea: Generic sub-agent delegation and parallel runs add nothing and can lose on fast-tier and mid-size models; one trained specialist component may differ.
best_evidence: GLM 5.2 medal rate 55.7% base, 45.2% with delegation, 33.3% with delegation and parallel runs (2609.40303 p7)
evidence_quality: weak: 14 tasks with wide intervals, none significant; other paper is the vendor's own harness
why: Two papers, newest September 2026, find delegation no better on fast tier and mid models. A trained specialist coder helped five models in 2610.11123, a different design.

idea: Single runs on 20 to 100 tasks cannot resolve gaps under about ten points, so many small-model harness gains sit inside run-to-run noise; repeat and publish intervals.
best_evidence: Rerunning the same arm moved its mean by up to 0.069 (2610.02001 p32)
evidence_quality: strong: several papers measure their own noise directly, intervals plus or minus 11 to 13 points, repeats varied up to 5.41 times
why: Several papers report their own repeat noise and intervals, newest October 2026, and none shows small-sample gaps being stable. This is a statement about method, not about models.

idea: Harness gains are largest for the weakest model that can still follow the output format; below that point the same harness gives nothing or hurts.
evidence_quality: weak: gains measured on authors' own tasks; the competence threshold is only argued, one supporting quote not found in text
why: Many papers see bigger gains for weaker models; others see negative or zero lift for the weakest. The split is plausible but no paper measures the threshold, and the newest gain claim has an unverified quote.

idea: A small model can write or evolve a harness only if trained for it; untrained weak writers lose most of the gain.
models: Llama3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5
best_evidence: Trained 9B editor 64.0% against 61.3% for frozen Opus-4.6 editor (2609.40330)
evidence_quality: weak: one side gives no numbers, other side authors' own tasks and a trained editor
why: An 8B rule writer trailed the learner by 0.235 on new contexts and weak self-written harnesses lost gain, yet a trained 9B editor matched Opus. The difference may be training, not size.

idea: Distilling a harness into the weights lets the harness be dropped at run time and can beat the harness attached, but not on every task.
best_evidence: Distilled Qwen3.5-9B 44.3% without harness against 41.7% with the evolved harness attached (2609.24974)
evidence_quality: weak: single runs, authors' own methods, mixed outcome inside one paper
why: Distilled student beat the attached harness on SpreadsheetBench 44.0 to 39.0 and AppWorld 58.9 to 48.2 but trailed on USPTO 30.0 to 38.0. A later activation-shift paper recovered half the gain in 8 of 10 settings.

idea: A small trained judge or step scorer can replace frontier verification at lower cost, but the saving depends on the generator model.
best_evidence: MiniMax-M2.7 76.40 at 2.26 times cost against 75.27 at 3.35 times; DeepSeek-V4-Flash no gain (2610.30284)
evidence_quality: weak: few papers, authors' own judge training, generator-dependent result, small samples
why: Four papers from September and October 2026 find trained small judges close to frontier ones for less cost, while one shows no accuracy gain on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. This separates from the controller result, which was untrained.

idea: Small models look safer under unsafe actions only because they skip steps or fail tasks; switching harness barely changes their vulnerability.
best_evidence: Qwen3.5-4B attack success 89.4% to 97.7% across five harnesses (2610.35188)
evidence_quality: medium: measured across five harnesses and many models, but attack suites built by the authors
why: Newest October 2026. Low leakage came from skipped steps, a 0.8B model damaged files in 99 of 100 runs, and no harness moved 4B attack success below 89.4%. Learned skill boundaries helped in one paper.

idea: With strong models, swapping among mature general coding harnesses moves score about as much as a rerun; it mostly moves token cost, up to three times; gaps shrink with more time.
best_evidence: Each harness changes the score by between -0.7 and +0.6 points while model means span 27.2 points (2611.10600 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: many independent benchmarks agree, but mostly one run per cell and no bare baseline; rerun noise rivals swaps
why: Many independent measurements from September to November on the strongest models agree; the contrary cases are weaker models and games, split into their own idea. Same as the first pass, now with much more support.

idea: A model's own vendor harness gives no consistent advantage over a shared harness; the best harness flips by model, so test the pairing.
best_evidence: Shared harness wins 11 of 20 pairs, native harness wins 9, none tied (2608.06301 page 11); native lowered five of seven models (2610.28679 page 4)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers across many models, same direction, but single runs and authors' own benchmarks
why: Measured repeatedly in autumn on the strongest models, signs differ by model in all of them. Two vendor-friendly cases exist (Qwen Code, ZeroClaw) but are authored by the vendor.

idea: Weaker open models and long-horizon or game tasks show large score gaps between harnesses, far above the near-null gap for strong models on coding tasks.
best_evidence: Qwen3.8-Max on Splendor 33.3% under OpenCode to 91.7% under Qwen Code, six of six scenarios (2610.35773 page 9)
evidence_quality: weak: mostly single runs, authors' own benchmarks, one author group makes the Qwen models tested, effect sizes vary by task
why: Several autumn measurements show large gaps on weaker models and multi-step games. Harness explains only 12 percent of variance in 2610.05778, so the effect is real but smaller than the headline gaps.

idea: For small open models, tool exposure mismatches cause large losses: calling a read tool the harness does not expose, tools hidden behind search, or definitions placed where the model ignores them.
best_evidence: Goose got 68 of 69 unavailable-tool calls for a read tool it did not expose, OpenCode none (2605.27922 page 8); 95 of 96 hidden-search episodes rejected (2610.05778 page 9)
evidence_quality: medium: mechanism counted in logs across several papers, but authors built benchmarks and no bare baseline
why: The mechanism is counted in logs and nothing contradicts it; the newest paper is from October on mid-size open models. Output caps moved to their own idea.

idea: Limits on tool output and reply length (completion caps, truncation, compaction) cause much of the loss between harnesses; truncation markers that tell the model how to narrow the query recover it.
best_evidence: 76.9% narrow the query after guided truncation versus 44.0% after bare truncation (2610.15093 page 7); half of OpenCode's 9-point gap is output-cap cut-offs (2610.04433 page 3)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers count the mechanism in logs, but one run per cell and authors built the benchmarks
why: New idea. Autumn papers with fixed budgets agree on the mechanism and none contradicts it; it explains part of the harness gaps in the first idea.

idea: A large visible tool menu lowers success, mostly through truncated replies, and costs tokens; narrowing candidate tools cuts cost, but hiding tool names behind a search step fails small models.
best_evidence: Menu of 8 to 128 schemas lowers success 17.5 points with full menu visible (2610.21098 page 6); menu penalty tracks truncation, r -0.95
evidence_quality: medium: 21 configurations, fixed budgets, exact grading, but one benchmark family and the router uses ground truth
why: Replaces the first-pass stale loading idea: a later large controlled study with fixed budgets found the menu penalty and traced it to truncation. Hidden-search counter-evidence is kept as a limit.

idea: Whether tools arrive through a protocol server or a command line sets neither score nor cost reliably; the choice matters only when the command line gives raw files the search tools lack.
best_evidence: Command-line access gains 7.85% average; Codex GPT-5.5 59.90% against 45.52% with protocol, Claude Opus 5.5 73.68% against 72.65% (2611.05512 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: older papers show a null with huge ratio spread, the newer shows gains on authors' own benchmark
why: An August null with paired ratios from 0.43 to 29.06 and a November gain disagree; I could not split them cleanly beyond the raw-file difference, so contested.

idea: A command that returns success without doing the action, such as a prompting command with closed input, misleads agents; a wrapper that reports the real effect removes most false successes.
best_evidence: Receipt completes 25 of 25 trap tasks, native Terminus 17 (2611.01930 page 11)
evidence_quality: weak: one paper, authors built the traps and the fix, old small models, one run in the main test
why: Measured, newest in the window, nothing contradicts it; a second paper shows a timed-out command running on for 45 seconds. Harm is built into the tasks.

idea: After a write times out agents create duplicate side effects; the tool contract decides, not model or harness: idempotency keys on every write cut duplicates from 28% to 4%.
best_evidence: Duplicate rate 28% to 4%; late-commit duplicates 61% to 9% with keys on every write (2609.29095 page 11)
evidence_quality: medium: 25,930 episodes on strong models and three harnesses, but simulated services and authors' own contract design
why: Large September measurement on the strongest models, natives equal the minimal scaffold, so only the contract changes the result. Authors' own fix, simulated services, exploratory analyses.

idea: On strong models, a plain shell plus file editing matches richer sets of overlapping generic tools; extra tools that repeat what the shell can do add tokens, not success.
best_evidence: Bash-only gave +3.6 points on SWE-Bench and cut cost 53% for Nemotron-3 550B (2609.20804 page 12)
evidence_quality: medium: many papers agree, but mostly one run, no bare baseline, no frontier model in the main case
why: First-pass contested idea split by regime: overlapping generic tools show no gain; the counter-papers add editing or capability tools, now a separate idea. The 2609.04280 gain compares to task-specific tools, not to a shell.

idea: Tools that give the model information or actions it cannot get from text alone, such as perception, a formal checker, a computation tool, or platform connectors, give large gains, especially for weaker models.
best_evidence: Claude Code completed 9 of 46 tasks alone, 39 with platform tools; Codex 9 alone, 35 (2611.07461 page 39)
evidence_quality: medium: many papers and a clear mechanism, but authors built tasks and tools and most have no repeated runs
why: Many autumn measurements on strongest models agree; the null cases are tools that wrap what a shell agent can already do. Gains of 9 to 39 come from an authors' own platform.

idea: A task-specific checker, compile-and-run probe or verifier tool carries most of a harness lift; generic self-critique adds little, and telling the policy a verifier will judge it can lower results.
best_evidence: Withdrawing the score tool lowered speedup significantly in 3 of 8 setups (2610.20673 page 6); probe 213 to 218 of 222 accepted (2609.15983 page 15)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers with bare or paired baselines, but gains are small on strong models and tools are authors' own
why: Mostly agreeing, newest October; the effect on strong models is only a few points, and the one contrary result concerns prompting about the verifier, not the checker itself.

idea: Single-shot search with the raw question as the query adds nothing over closed-book answering; the gain comes from search the model iterates, and from indexes that return only the slice asked for.
best_evidence: Gold paper found for 6% of claims; accuracy no better than closed-book (2610.29812 page 3); BRIGHT recall 8.41% single-shot against 49.59% iterative (2605.05538 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: two papers on different tasks, same direction, but small search-lite models and authors' own benchmarks
why: Measured October on light hosted models, nothing of equal quality contradicts it; a section-index failure on GPT-5.2 is a different mechanism. Depth-at-chosen-pixel result moved out of this idea.

idea: Giving a strong model the data as files with a shell or code matches or beats pre-built query and search tools, and is cheaper; the gain needs several turns of programming, not one script.
best_evidence: Python over node and edge files 75.2 against 72.8 for predefined graph tools, one program 69.0 (2610.18616 page 6 and 7)
evidence_quality: weak: gains of 1 to 8 points, one run in the graph paper, authors' own benchmarks, the Claude Code gap is one point
why: New idea. Two autumn papers on strong models agree on direction, with the largest effect on cost; the Claude Code gap is small, so I do not call the effect large.

idea: Small models need natural-language, typed or structured tool layers; forcing them to write raw code or free-form actions collapses success, while strong models cope with free-form code.
best_evidence: Removing the natural-language tool layer drops ToolBench pass rate from 75.1 to 16.1 for Qwen3-8B (2609.01736 page 8)
evidence_quality: weak: few papers on 8B or smaller trained models, authors built tasks, trial counts missing in one
why: New idea. Measured on small models up to October, nothing contradicts it; the strong-model side comes from the files-and-code idea above.

idea: Moving a model from chat-only to a coding-agent environment with shell, files and iteration gives the largest effect on tasks that need running code or checking results.
best_evidence: Single-shot 73.6% to agentic 95.1% for qwen3.7-plus (2610.35138 page 1); bare adapter 19.3 to full adapter 71.2 for GLM 5.1 (2606.12344 page 9)
evidence_quality: medium: several papers across strengths, large effect, but authors' own tasks and the chat number in 2609.40303 is missing
why: Large effects on tasks that need execution, measured in October on strong models; the document-reading null is split into its own idea. First pass kept.

idea: For document-reading reconstruction tasks, strong models run as native coding agents with tools do not measurably beat calling the same models directly.
best_evidence: Mean paired differences +0.033 Claude, +0.005 GPT, -0.030 Gemini, all padj = 1.000 (2610.37851 page 5)
evidence_quality: medium: three strong models, direct-call baseline, paired test, but single runs and only 20 protocols
why: Newest evidence on the strongest models with a bare baseline and corrected tests. Counter-paper 2610.35138 is code editing, a different task type.

idea: Where a structured command or application path exists, routing the agent to it beats driving the screen; computer use in place of a shell cut resolution from 21.4% to 3.6% for GPT-6 Astra.
best_evidence: Computer use 3.6% against 21.4% for the shell setup in Codex CLI (2609.35143 page 6)
evidence_quality: medium: one clean same-model comparison on 56 tasks, one run each, plus older agreeing papers
why: New idea. Sept measurement on the strongest model, nothing newer contradicts it; the screen route only wins on visually grounded single-app tasks, listed as the limit.

idea: Small trained models are brittle to the format and order of observations and actions and to their training harness: reversing field order cut success sharply; another harness cut it too.
best_evidence: Reversing observation field order cut task success from 85.0% to 19.2% (2610.37255 page 2)
evidence_quality: weak: papers on trained small models, authors built tasks, effects specific to each trained model
why: Measured after September in several papers with nothing against it, but only for trained small models. Re-judged with three more papers than the first pass.

idea: Giving a model verified, fresh tool-health state before each action cuts regret and failed completions against a neutral control of the same shape.
best_evidence: Mean regret 4,251.54 ms to 131.12 ms; completion 50/72 to 69/72 (2611.05391 page 5)
evidence_quality: weak: one paper, authors built benchmark and penalty metric, no retries, 9 live decisions per condition
why: Measured with a same-shape control on three frontier models, dated September; nothing contradicts it. Single paper, tiny sample, so held at weak.

idea: Automatic edits to tool descriptions and tool code raise pass rate on the tasks and agent they were tuned on, but the gain does not transfer across agents, and description rewrites alone can lower reward.
best_evidence: Cross-agent averages show no significant reward gain; Telecom 29.50% to 36.75% for tool-code edits, a documentation rewrite lowered it to 25.58% (2610.34679 page 6 and 7)
evidence_quality: medium: one paper with 30 trials and paired tests, but only one of three benchmarks significant and authors' own optimizer
why: Same-agent gains (14.2 held-out lift in 2609.05736) and a cross-agent null from 2610.34679 conflict, and I could not separate them by regime given one optimizer run per domain.

idea: Whether exact-text search or vector search wins in an agent flips with the harness and with whether results print inline or go to files; do not choose from one benchmark.
best_evidence: Opus 4.6 scored 93.1% on Chronos but 76.7% on Claude Code with the same inline grep (2605.15184 page 4)
evidence_quality: weak: one paper, 116 questions, no repeats, authors' own harness, no no-search baseline
why: Measured only in May on models later papers no longer treat as strongest; the November protocol-versus-files paper did not re-test search type.

idea: A structural code index with call graph and meaning search inside a coding agent raises file hit rate and resolved tasks over grep alone, most on multi-file changes.
best_evidence: Resolve 41.9% to 50.4%, +7.9 points, p = 0.003, 80 paired instances (2606.22417 page 7)
evidence_quality: weak: one model, authors built the agent, no bare arm; gap versus OpenCode not significant p = 0.087
why: Both supporting papers predate September on Opus 4.6 and 4.7. Later tool ablations on Claude Opus 5 moved nothing, though they did not test an index.

idea: Wrapping a frontier model in a naive tool-using agent lowers its score compared with a single pass.
best_evidence: Single-pass 58.61% versus agent 47.39% (2603.19347 page 3)
evidence_quality: weak: the two conditions used different task subsets; one benchmark, no significance test
why: Later better-controlled work found agents equal (document reconstruction) or better (code editing, 73.6% to 95.1%). The earlier gap was confounded by different task subsets.

idea: A model told to re-check, reflect on or grade its own work, with no new outside information, does not raise success and sometimes discards correct work.
models: Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.6 Terra, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, Claude Haiku 5.5
best_evidence: Always-verify instruction 11/28 passed, same as the 11/28 baseline, 2609.26048 page 5
evidence_quality: medium: seven papers on several models agree; samples small, several single runs, no repeats in some
why: Later strong-model measurements (September to October) still find no gain from self-review; the favourable confidence-steered retry paper is from May and uses a different mechanism with outside signal.

idea: A separate critic or a different coding product, given the task and the changes, raises accuracy at modest extra cost; self-review at completion time does not.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.6, Claude Opus 5, GLM-5.2
best_evidence: Independent critic review gave +5.9 to +9.5 points on Terminal-Bench at 1.13 to 1.25 times cost, 2610.34577 page 8
evidence_quality: medium: six papers, strong models, concrete deltas; three trials per cell, no bare baseline, authors' own tasks
why: Reviewers that see the work and run checks beat self-checking in September to October measurements on strong models; the null result (2610.19591) reviews single shell calls, a different job, so it sits under per-action review.

idea: Per-action review, where a reviewer model approves or blocks each tool call, may cut rule violations in a rule-heavy domain but showed no pass-rate gain on shell work.
best_evidence: Reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4%, over-refusals 1.6% to 1.4%, 2611.06116 page 7
evidence_quality: weak: one episode per case, authors built bank and scorer, no bare baseline; null paper has 37 tasks, three attempts
why: A gain on a policy-violation bank on 2026-11-04 against no significant effect on shell calls (pass at three 41.7 versus 40.5 to 43.2) and extra false rejections from a judge defence; floor effect plausible, untested.

idea: Concrete outside feedback that names what failed (test results, execution output, diagnosis routed to the owning component) raises success far above no feedback, and detailed feedback beats minimal.
best_evidence: Removing diagnosis feedback cut Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 51.8% to 41.2%, 2611.07461 page 26
evidence_quality: medium: many removal ablations on strong models; mostly authors' own systems, single runs, no bare baseline
why: Newest measurement on a strong model confirms it; the two small effects (language server diagnostics +3.7 on qwen3.6-flash, full scoring feedback lowering two open models) concern feedback quality, covered by the next idea.

idea: More feedback or more repair rounds is not monotone: gains flatten after about three rounds, redundant verification multiplies cost with no success gain, and over-rich or fused feedback can lower success.
best_evidence: Raising repair turns from 3 to 5 lowered Opus 4.7 validity from 0.81 to 0.78, 2606.03005 page 9
evidence_quality: medium: five papers agree on different tasks; the newest is a small model and the strongest-model result is from June
why: No measurement shows unlimited rounds helping; the newest dated 2026-09-01 on a small model, and the Opus 4.7 result is a June measurement, so the ceiling for newest models is unretested.

idea: A deterministic or executable checker that verifies and repairs a plan or output lifts small and mid models strongly where the bare model is weak, and beats feedback-only replanning.
best_evidence: Qwen3-8B success rose from 41.2% to 91.8% with graph verification, 2609.19315 page 1
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own checkers, mostly single seeds, one household benchmark carries the biggest number
why: Seven papers from August to November on small and mid models all show large gains where the bare rate is low and the check is exact; none contradict. Gains depend on a checkable world.

idea: Retrying a small model with plain error text helps a lot on some tasks and nothing on others; test per task whether a retry loop pays off for a small local model.
best_evidence: Qwen3-14B went from 17.53% to 66.99% with execution revision, 2610.30917 page 6
evidence_quality: weak: authors' own harnesses, single seeds, 30 tasks in the negative kernel case, no intervals
why: Revision helped every Qwen model from 1.7B to 27B in one paper; a 7B kernel agent, an 8B patch agent and a DeepSeek V3.2 puzzle solver gained nothing. Task type and feedback usefulness differ; no paper isolates the cause.

idea: When several candidates can be sampled, choosing among them with a real executed check or critique signal recovers part of the gap to the best candidate; model opinion alone leaves most of it.
best_evidence: Best of eight with a real evaluator: 3% to 33% correct, 7B model, 2611.12079 page 1
evidence_quality: medium: six papers with controlled candidate pools; several are authors' benchmarks, one model each
why: Real checks pick better than model opinion in measurements to November. Against: decision-only verification lowered two of three model sizes, and one paper found generation, not ranking, the limit.

idea: Letting a model accept its own harness edits without an outside held-out check makes the harness drift worse; an outside gate with fresh-context critic and rollback stops it.
models: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
best_evidence: Accepting every revision: training success fell from 42% to 34% in ten rounds, 2609.39304 page 3
evidence_quality: medium: eight papers, different systems, strong and small models agree; small task sets and the authors' own methods
why: Eight systems from July to November show regression or lost held-out score without a gate, newest dated 2026-11-02 on a mid model; none report an ungated loop that held up.

idea: A held-out gate on harness edits does not reliably keep good edits and reject bad ones: gated harnesses have ended below the starting harness or lost held-out score, and validation rank poorly predicts test rank.
models: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, Kimi-K3
best_evidence: Gated harness scored 64.04% against initial 67.98% on OfficeQA certification, 2609.18366 page 9
evidence_quality: weak: one run per method, wide intervals, no bare baseline, gate tests and selection rules chosen after the fact
why: Picking by development score gained 4.53 held-out points in one study, yet fixed gates lost to the start harness, and Kimi-K3 lost held-out score on two domains. Gate quality and set size differ; no regime split found.

idea: A same-strength or weaker model grading holistically or by pairwise preference is unreliable: position bias, self-preference, inflated scores, and it overrates flawed runs; it cannot be the only grader.
models: Claude Opus 5.5, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT 4.1 Nano
best_evidence: Same-strength judge pooled reliability against gold 48%, 50% positional flips, 2608.13608 page 12
evidence_quality: medium: six papers across tasks agree; the strong-model evidence is one 3.4 point preference and one position-bias figure
why: Position bias (81 percent second-shown) and self-preference appear on weak and on Claude Opus 5.5 judges through October; strong rubric-based judges are a separate, favourable idea.

idea: A strong judge scoring each checklist or rubric item separately, with a reference or rendered evidence, agrees with human labels in roughly 83 to 96 percent of cases.
models: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.8 Flash
best_evidence: Judge agreed with humans on 95.8% of 264 judgments, 2611.05512 page 12
evidence_quality: medium: four recent papers with human reference labels; authors built the benchmarks and checklists, one judge model each
why: Newest agreement figures from November on frontier judges are high and consistent; contested pairs fall to 70.7 percent and agreement with humans is not the same as catching faults.

idea: An agent's own report that it finished or verified its work is unreliable on strong models; a read-only outside check of real files, state or output catches false completion.
models: Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, claude-opus-5
best_evidence: Enforced checks: 8 of 8 agents reproduced headline numbers against 1 of 8 unchecked, 2609.23957 page 21
evidence_quality: medium: many papers on strong models agree; one run per task and authors' own tasks mostly
why: All 35 closing reports of 45 failed Terminal-Bench 4 tasks claimed every requirement verified, and 93 percent of runs claimed success on another benchmark; no paper finds self-reports reliable.

idea: Passing the project's own tests, compiling or producing the file is a weak signal of acceptable work; a separate quality or acceptance gate rejects many test-passing results.
best_evidence: 562 of 771 unresolved runs failed only the quality test, 2609.35143 page 7
evidence_quality: medium: eight measured papers across domains agree; authors' own gates and benchmarks, one run per task
why: Measurements to mid-November on strong models agree; only a March mutation study on Claude Sonnet 4.5 found visible tests adequate, older and narrower.

idea: A deterministic gate that admits only findings backed by a citation or a reproduced witness raises precision and cuts unsafe actions, but strict gates also drop real findings and can yield nothing.
models: Claude Opus 4.8, GLM-5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5
best_evidence: Direct runs gave 3.2 times more false positives than the harness, precision 90.0 to 96.9%, 2610.04243 page 1
evidence_quality: medium: six papers across code and security tasks agree on precision; authors' own benchmarks, mostly single runs
why: Fewer false findings in every October measurement; the cost is recall (680 of 1,232 excluded reports were real; 245 agents gave zero findings) and one blind human review saw no difference in real-bug rate.

idea: Verifiers and tests written by the model are themselves unreliable: they reject correct work more often than they reject wrong work, and some pass wrong work, so they need checking against reference solutions.
best_evidence: Generated verifiers accepted valid solutions only 21.1% to 70.2% of the time, 2610.28679 page 2
evidence_quality: medium: 19 models in one study plus a second paper agree; one generation per configuration, authors built the benchmark
why: Replaces the June idea that about a fifth of reproduction tests were wrong: November measurements on stronger models find more false rejections, 87.9 to 96.0 percent from verifiers that reject every case.

idea: Whether a verification or context add-on helps depends on the model: it can raise false reports or lower accuracy on mid-tier models while helping frontier ones, or the reverse.
best_evidence: GLM-5.1 false reports rose 13.3% to 29.4% while GPT-5.5 fell 10.0% to 5.3%, 2610.28802 page 12
evidence_quality: medium: six papers report model-specific signs; mostly one run or one episode per cell
why: Each measurement from September to November shows effects differing by model and none a uniform effect; test every add-on on the model in use.

idea: Fixes for one failure often break behaviour that worked, and models predict their own regressions near chance, so replaying earlier cases before accepting a change is needed.
best_evidence: Replay rejected 383 proposed rules, 211 (55%) fixed the trigger yet regressed protected behaviour, 2609.24130 page 5
evidence_quality: medium: real replay decisions plus a regression-source breakdown; no matched control run without replay
why: Verification conflicts were 87.1 percent of pass-to-fail cases in November; prediction precision 11.8 percent in April. No paper disagrees.

idea: A finish gate that checks outside evidence before handoff gives small to moderate gains on strong models, but the gain is uncertain: some tests find no effect or a null controller.
models: GPT-5.5 xhigh, MiniMax-M2.7, GPT-OSS-20B, Claude Sonnet 5.5
best_evidence: Handoff gate took one task from 0/5 to 5/5, called an association not an ablation, 2608.15089 page 17
evidence_quality: weak: gains are 2 to 6 points with intervals crossing zero or tiny samples; null results have equal budgets and placebo
why: Reworded from the June-era claim that gates only add cost. A trained selective gate gained 1.7 points at 1.09 times cost, yet a nine-billion model's exit gate and a cheap controller moved nothing; model strength decides.

idea: Diagnosis that names the failing component and routes the failure back raises repair success; free-text self-reflection finds the region but rarely the cause.
best_evidence: Typed diagnosis repaired 114 of 120 injected defects against 4 of 120 for regeneration without feedback, 2608.28363 page 7
evidence_quality: medium: four papers agree on structured diagnosis; injected defects, authors' own benchmarks, one backbone each
why: Newest dated 2026-11-05 on a strong model; the one dissent shows grounded diagnosis lowering recovery by 6.29 points on a stratum that already worked.

idea: A check that a cited source exists is not enough; verify that the cited evidence supports the claim, since models cite real sources that are irrelevant or never retrieved.
best_evidence: Closed-book models cited identifiers that exist but only 1 of 186 was judged relevant, 2610.29812 page 4
evidence_quality: medium: four papers in October agree across models; judges are models, benchmarks authors' own
why: Four independent October measurements on strong models show existence checks pass while support is missing; checking each finding against its cited evidence added 16.0 points on one benchmark.

idea: Strong agents can game or tamper with weak verifiers, so verification evidence must sit outside agent reach and trajectories need audit; on strong models the measured effect has been small.
best_evidence: Commitment seal blocked 14 of 14 modified candidates from being frozen against 0 of 14 without it, 2610.26101 page 26
evidence_quality: weak: staged tampering cases and one audited trial; one trial of 445 removed on Opus 5
why: Seeded tampering was caught 90.4 percent by an auditor and a seal blocked all staged edits, but a real audit removed only 1 of 445 rewarded trials; the risk is real, the size on strong models small.

idea: Rubric or verifier-guided revision of open-ended outputs beats direct generation, and the detail of the reviewer feedback matters more than self-checking or more reasoning.
best_evidence: Rubric-guided revision gave a 10.05 point mean gain across model-harness setups, 2611.06506 page 1
evidence_quality: medium: five papers on text, image and design tasks agree; authors' benchmarks and judges, no repeats stated in several
why: Newest measurements to November agree across ten setups; the dissent is that most feedback baselines without a verifier did not beat direct generation, and a stronger editor gained less from a coding harness.

idea: Stacking several gates adds less than independent-error maths predicts, because gates share blind spots; changing verifier model family or evidence source is argued to raise the ceiling.
best_evidence: Independence extrapolation understates failure 20 times at five gates, synthetic data only, 2607.13918 page 6
evidence_quality: weak: theory plus synthetic data; no real model or task, and the practical claims are argued
why: Only a mathematical model on synthetic data supports it; the real-model hint (pairing different coding products cut silent defects from 35.4% to 10.4%) does not test correlation directly.
